This guide walks through implementing Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) in Soroban smart contracts. It covers storing role assignments, restricting functions to specific roles, granting and revoking roles securely, and testing role-based access restrictions. Prerequisites Rust and cargo Soroban CLI and soroban_sdk Familiarity with the require_auth() pattern Goals Implement explicit roles for managing different levels of access. Securely store role assignments on-chain. Safely grant and revoke roles to and from users. Role Storage and Enforcement Role storage​ Roles should be stored securely in the contract's persistent storage. Using an enum for roles ensures strict typing. The data key should map an Address to their assigned Role. Granting and revoking roles​ Role assignment should be restricted to administrators. The grant_role and revoke_role functions must require the admin's authorization before modifying the persistent storage. Security Note: If the sole administrator role is compromised, the attacker can grant themselves any role, escalate privileges, and lock out legitimate users (admin takeover). Ensure the administrator role is properly secured, for example by using a multi-sig account or a governance contract. Enforcement​ The has_role helper reads from storage to check if an address holds a specific role. The require_role function wraps this to return an Error::Unauthorized if the check fails. Using structured errors instead of panicking allows callers to handle denials gracefully. Contract Tests Unaudited learning example This RBAC contract is unaudited teaching material and is not production-ready. Do not deploy it with real funds or privileges without a full security review, threat model, storage-lifetime plan, and tests for your exact authorization model. Reentrancy is not exercised in this page because the shown functions only read/write this contract's storage and do not call external contracts. If you add token transfers, callbacks, or other cross-contract calls, re-check the order of authorization, state changes, and external calls. Role assignments are stored in persistent storage. Persistent entries still have ledger TTL and can expire unless the contract or an external maintenance flow bumps them, so production RBAC needs a clear data-expiry policy for admin and role records. // See examples/access-control/src/lib.rs for the complete example #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contracterror, contractimpl, contracttype, Address, Env}; #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub enum Role { User, Manager, Admin, } #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone)] pub enum DataKey { Role(Address), } #[contracterror] #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq, PartialOrd, Ord)] #[repr(u32)] pub enum Error { Unauthorized = 1, } pub fn has_role(env: &Env, user: &Address, role: Role) -> bool { env.storage() .persistent() .get::<DataKey, Role>(&DataKey::Role(user.clone())) .map(|stored| stored == role) .unwrap_or(false) } pub fn require_role(env: &Env, user: &Address, role: Role) -> Result<(), Error> { if has_role(env, user, role) { Ok(()) } else { Err(Error::Unauthorized) } } #[contract] pub struct AccessControl; #[contractimpl] impl AccessControl { pub fn __constructor(env: Env, admin: Address) { env.storage() .persistent() .set(&DataKey::Role(admin), &Role::Admin); } pub fn grant_role(env: Env, granter: Address, user: Address, role: Role) -> Result<(), Error> { granter.require_auth(); require_role(&env, &granter, Role::Admin)?; env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Role(user), &role); Ok(()) } pub fn revoke_role(env: Env, granter: Address, user: Address) -> Result<(), Error> { granter.require_auth(); require_role(&env, &granter, Role::Admin)?; env.storage().persistent().remove(&DataKey::Role(user)); Ok(()) } pub fn manager_only_action(env: Env, caller: Address) -> Result<(), Error> { caller.require_auth(); require_role(&env, &caller, Role::Manager) } } Testing non-admin denial​ It is crucial to test that non-admins cannot perform restricted actions or grant roles to others. #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; use soroban_sdk::testutils::Address as _; #[test] fn test_non_admin_is_denied_admin_only_action() { let (env, _, client) = setup(); let outsider = Address::generate(&env); let result = client.try_admin_only_action(&outsider); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::Unauthorized))); } #[test] fn test_non_admin_cannot_grant_roles() { let (env, _, client) = setup(); let alice = Address::generate(&env); let bob = Address::generate(&env); let result = client.try_grant_role(&alice, &bob, &Role::Manager); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::Unauthorized))); assert_eq!(client.get_role(&bob), None); } } Related code Access Control Example Authorization Pattern

This guide describes secure authorization and access-control patterns for Soroban smart contracts. It covers common patterns (role-based, capability-based), where to place checks, insecure anti-patterns, and guidance for testing authorization paths. The examples/authorization crate is the canonical reference implementation for this page. It demonstrates a two-tier owner/admin model using require_auth(), with the pattern implemented and tested in a compact, auditable form. Unaudited Example Code The example code in this pattern is for educational purposes and has not been audited for production use. Always conduct a thorough security audit before deploying to mainnet. Prerequisites Rust and cargo Soroban CLI and soroban_sdk Familiarity with Address and require_auth() semantics Goals Make authorization checks explicit and auditable. Keep capability boundaries small and verifiable. Prefer least-privilege defaults and fail-safe behavior. Crate walkthrough: examples/authorization The examples/authorization/src/lib.rs crate implements a minimal, two-tier ownership model: Entrypoint Auth required Purpose initialize(owner) None (call-once pattern) Store the owner address in persistent storage set_admin(admin) owner.require_auth() Owner-gated admin assignment privileged_action() admin.require_auth() Admin-gated privileged operation Current scope​ The crate intentionally covers the foundational require_auth() pattern. The following capabilities are documented gaps — tracked for future expansion: Sub-invocation authorization (require_auth_for_args) — restricting authorization to a specific function signature and argument tuple, preventing authorization replay across calls. Authorization trees — verifying auth from nested contract-to-contract calls (cross-contract invoke chains). Custom accounts — contracts that implement custom signature verification (e.g., multisig wallets that satisfy require_auth() through __check_auth). Role-based access control (RBAC) — a richer Role enum (Admin, Manager, User) with a has_role/require_role guard. See the companion examples/access-control crate for a full RBAC implementation. Patterns Role-based access​ Store a small, explicit mapping from an Address to role identifiers. Check role membership at the edge of functions that modify sensitive state. See the tested access-control example for a complete role-based access control (RBAC) implementation: a Role enum (Admin, Manager, User), role assignments held in env.storage().persistent(), and a reusable has_role/require_role check used to guard restricted entry points. For production patterns that compose role-based access control with emergency circuit breakers, see the tested pausable-token example. Capability-based access​ Give callers limited capabilities (tokens, allowances, or dedicated contract entries) instead of broad, single-administrator accounts. Capabilities can be revoked or rotated without changing primary keys. Check early, check often​ Perform authorization checks at public entry points (before expensive work) and re-check invariants when crossing capability boundaries. Principle of least privilege​ Keep privileged operations narrow and minimize the number of privileged addresses or capabilities. Contract Contract (Secure) Tests Insecure: implicit or scattered checks​ #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, Env, Address}; #[contract] pub struct Bad; #[contractimpl] impl Bad { // Uses a single global flag and scattered checks — easy to misuse or forget. pub fn set_admin(env: Env, admin: Address) { // No access control here — anyone can call env.storage().persistent().set(&"admin", &admin); } pub fn privileged_action(env: Env) { // Check is scattered and easy to omit in other methods let admin: Address = env.storage().persistent().get(&"admin").unwrap(); if !env.invoker().eq(&admin) { panic!("unauthorized"); } // do privileged work } } This pattern fails if initialization is incorrect, or if other methods forget the check. Secure: explicit role mapping and require_auth()​ The following matches the actual examples/authorization/src/lib.rs implementation exactly: #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, Address, Env}; #[contract] pub struct AccessControl; #[contractimpl] impl AccessControl { pub fn initialize(env: Env, owner: Address) { // initialization should be controlled (callable only once in practice) env.storage().persistent().set(&"owner", &owner); } fn owner_of(env: &Env) -> Address { env.storage().persistent().get(&"owner").unwrap() } pub fn set_admin(env: Env, admin: Address) { // Require the owner to sign before changing admin let owner = Self::owner_of(&env); owner.require_auth(); env.storage().persistent().set(&"admin", &admin); } pub fn privileged_action(env: Env) { let admin: Address = env.storage().persistent().get(&"admin").unwrap(); admin.require_auth(); // safely perform privileged work } } Key points: Use Address::require_auth() to assert caller identity. Keep mapping keys explicit and minimal (owner, admin, or a small role map). Prefer dedicated setter methods guarded by the highest privilege. Documented gaps in this crate: require_auth_for_args is not yet demonstrated — it further restricts authorization to a specific function+args tuple. Auth trees (cross-contract require_auth propagation) are not covered. Custom accounts (__check_auth) are not covered. The tests below match the actual test suite in examples/authorization/src/lib.rs: #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; use soroban_sdk::{testutils::Address as _, Env}; #[test] fn test_initialize_and_set_admin() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register(AccessControl, ()); let client = AccessControlClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let owner = Address::generate(&env); let alice = Address::generate(&env); env.mock_all_auths(); client.initialize(&owner); client.set_admin(&alice); } #[test] fn test_privileged_action() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register(AccessControl, ()); let client = AccessControlClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let owner = Address::generate(&env); let alice = Address::generate(&env); env.mock_all_auths(); client.initialize(&owner); client.set_admin(&alice); client.privileged_action(); } } Anti-patterns Relying on env.invoker() checks scattered throughout code without enforcing signing (require_auth is safer). Granting a single address unlimited rights without revocation or rotation plan. Mixing business logic and authorization checks in many places instead of centralizing them. Testing Authorization Paths Unit tests: assert both authorized and unauthorized callers for every public method. Edge cases: test initialization, role rotation, and revocation flows. Property/fuzz testing: ensure that random inputs cannot bypass checks. Use env.mock_all_auths() carefully to ensure you still assert require_auth() behavior where relevant. Audit and Review Keep the role map small and well-documented. Document the capability boundaries in the contract README. Consider off-chain governance flows for role changes. A balance snapshot records the balance of each holder at a defined ledger. It lets an application calculate a deterministic airdrop or dividend entitlement without trusting balances that may change after the distribution is announced. The balance-snapshot example is a balance-accounting pattern: it focuses on historical holdings. The token-snapshot pattern adds token-specific snapshot metadata, total supply, and claim tracking for governance or reward claims. Concern Balance snapshot Token snapshot Primary use Airdrops, dividends, audit checkpoints Governance and claimable rewards Value captured Holder balance at a ledger Holder balance plus snapshot metadata Claim tracking Application-specific Contract-level claimed state
Create the snapshot before announcing the distribution, use the recorded ledger as the immutable cutoff, and bound the holder set so snapshot creation does not exceed the transaction resource budget.

This pattern demonstrates a complete basic token contract implementing three core operations: mint, transfer, and balance. It serves as the foundation for understanding token mechanics in Soroban before advancing to standardized token interfaces like SAC (Soroban Asset Contract). When to use Use this pattern to bootstrap a simple token system, understand state management for balances, and grasp authorization patterns. For production, consider using SAC or wrapping existing assets. Teaching Token The examples/token-transfer example demonstrates a teaching token implementation. It is not the Stellar Asset Contract (SAC) used for production assets. For production, refer to the Stellar Asset Contract (SAC) documentation. Prerequisites Rust stable and cargo Soroban CLI installed (setup guide) Basic familiarity with Soroban contracts and the soroban_sdk Understanding of Address types and authentication Implementation The contract manages a ledger mapping addresses to token balances using persistent storage. Three public functions allow minting tokens, querying balances, and transferring between accounts. Unaudited teaching example The contract below is an unaudited educational example. It has not been through a security review and it is not fit for production or for holding real value — most obviously because mint is completely unrestricted, so anyone can inflate the supply at will. Read the two limits that matter most before you copy anything: Reentrancy — none of mint, balance, or transfer makes a cross-contract call, so there is no re-entrant call to defend against as written. The moment you add one (a transfer-fee hook, a mint callback, a cross-chain message), that protection is gone. See Reentrancy limits. Storage TTL / data expiry — balances live in persistent storage, which expires. This example never extends a TTL, so a balance can be archived and then permanently deleted, silently turning into a zero balance. See Reentrancy and storage TTL limits. For a real token, use the Stellar Asset Contract (SAC) or the SEP-41 standard instead of deploying this. Contract Running Tests #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contracterror, contractimpl, contracttype, Address, Env}; /// Storage key for tracking token balances per address. #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone)] pub enum DataKey { Balance(Address), } /// Error codes for token operations. #[contracterror] #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq, PartialOrd, Ord)] #[repr(u32)] pub enum Error { InsufficientBalance = 1, InvalidAmount = 2, SelfTransfer = 3, } #[contract] pub struct TokenTransfer; #[contractimpl] impl TokenTransfer { /// Mint tokens to an address (for testing and bootstrapping). /// In production, restrict this to authorized minters. pub fn mint(env: Env, to: Address, amount: i128) { let key = DataKey::Balance(to.clone()); let current: i128 = env.storage().persistent().get(&key).unwrap_or(0); env.storage().persistent().set(&key, &(current + amount)); } /// Query the token balance of an address. pub fn balance(env: Env, of: Address) -> i128 { let key = DataKey::Balance(of); env.storage().persistent().get(&key).unwrap_or(0) } /// Transfer tokens from sender to recipient. /// Requires authorization from the sender address. pub fn transfer(env: Env, from: Address, to: Address, amount: i128) -> Result<(), Error> { from.require_auth(); // Validate amount if amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } // Prevent self-transfer if from == to { return Err(Error::SelfTransfer); } // Check sender has sufficient balance let from_key = DataKey::Balance(from.clone()); let from_balance: i128 = env.storage().persistent().get(&from_key).unwrap_or(0); if from_balance < amount { return Err(Error::InsufficientBalance); } // Perform transfer let to_key = DataKey::Balance(to.clone()); let to_balance: i128 = env.storage().persistent().get(&to_key).unwrap_or(0); env.storage() .persistent() .set(&from_key, &(from_balance - amount)); env.storage() .persistent() .set(&to_key, &(to_balance + amount)); Ok(()) } } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; use soroban_sdk::{testutils::Address as _, Env}; fn setup() -> (Env, TokenTransferClient<'static>) { let env = Env::default(); env.mock_all_auths(); let contract_id = env.register(TokenTransfer, ()); let client = TokenTransferClient::new(&env, &contract_id); (env, client) } #[test] fn test_mint_increases_balance() { let (env, client) = setup(); let alice = Address::generate(&env); client.mint(&alice, &500); assert_eq!(client.balance(&alice), 500); } #[test] fn test_transfer_moves_tokens() { let (env, client) = setup(); let alice = Address::generate(&env); let bob = Address::generate(&env); client.mint(&alice, &1000); client.transfer(&alice, &bob, &400); assert_eq!(client.balance(&alice), 600); assert_eq!(client.balance(&bob), 400); } #[test] fn test_transfer_fails_on_insufficient_balance() { let (env, client) = setup(); let alice = Address::generate(&env); let bob = Address::generate(&env); client.mint(&alice, &100); let result = client.try_transfer(&alice, &bob, &200); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::InsufficientBalance))); assert_eq!(client.balance(&alice), 100); assert_eq!(client.balance(&bob), 0); } #[test] fn test_transfer_fails_on_invalid_amount() { let (env, client) = setup(); let alice = Address::generate(&env); let bob = Address::generate(&env); client.mint(&alice, &100); let result = client.try_transfer(&alice, &bob, &0); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::InvalidAmount))); let result = client.try_transfer(&alice, &bob, &-50); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::InvalidAmount))); } #[test] fn test_self_transfer_is_rejected() { let (env, client) = setup(); let alice = Address::generate(&env); client.mint(&alice, &100); let result = client.try_transfer(&alice, &alice, &50); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::SelfTransfer))); } #[test] fn test_initial_balance_is_zero() { let (env, client) = setup(); let alice = Address::generate(&env); assert_eq!(client.balance(&alice), 0); } } Run the example tests to verify the implementation: cd examples/token-transfer cargo test Expected output: 6 passing tests covering mint, transfer, balance, validation, and edge cases. Key Concepts Storage Model​ Balances are stored in persistent storage using the Balance(Address) enum variant as the key. This allows efficient lookups and updates without scanning the entire ledger. Authorization​ The transfer function calls from.require_auth() to ensure the transaction is signed by the sender. This prevents unauthorized token transfers. Error Handling​ Three error codes cover the main failure modes: InsufficientBalance: Sender doesn't have enough tokens InvalidAmount: Zero or negative amounts are rejected SelfTransfer: Transferring to yourself is a no-op and disallowed Minting​ The mint function bypasses authorization checks. In production, restrict minting to authorized parties using a minter role or ownership model. Reentrancy and storage TTL limits These two limits are the difference between a teaching contract and a token that can safely hold value. Neither is enforced by this example. Reentrancy limits​ Reentrancy does not apply as written, and that is the only reason. mint, balance, and transfer call env.storage() and nothing else — there is no cross-contract call, no token transfer, and no callback, so no external code ever regains control partway through a state update. Soroban runs an invocation to completion unless a contract deliberately calls into another contract. The guarantees you can rely on today, and what breaks them: transfer is checks-then-effects. It reads the sender balance, verifies from_balance >= amount, and only then writes both sides. That ordering is safe only because no untrusted code runs between the read and the write. Adding any external call breaks it. Insert a transfer-fee hook, a mint callback, a cross-chain invoke_contract, or a SAC payment between the read and the write and the pattern is exploitable: re-read both balances after the call, because the callee can move funds or change state in the meantime. to_balance is read before the write. That value can be stale if anything external ran in between. Re-read it after any external call. transfer does call from.require_auth() — that is an authorization check, not a reentrancy guard. It stops unauthorized senders; it does not stop a callee re-entering. Use the repo's guard shape. The Reentrancy Guard pattern sets a storage flag before any external work and clears it afterwards, so a re-entrant call panics rather than double-spending. Adopt it whenever you extend this contract. Storage TTL and data-expiry limits​ Balances are stored with env.storage().persistent(), and persistent entries expire. This is the single most dangerous omission in the example: Nothing here extends a TTL. There is no extend_ttl call anywhere in the contract, so each balance entry gets the network's default minimum lifetime and then starts counting down. Expiry is two-phase. When a persistent entry's TTL lapses, the ledger archives it: reads still succeed but return the archived (stale) value while restoration is pending. If it is not restored before the next ledger closes the retention window, the entry is deleted permanently. A deleted balance reads back as 0. Because balance uses .unwrap_or(0), permanent deletion is indistinguishable from "never had a balance". A holder's funds can vanish with no error and no event. Instance storage would not help. Instance entries expire with the contract instance, so a long-idle token loses everything at once. A production token must extend the TTL on every balance it touches, extend it for a minimum window ahead of expiry, restore archived entries on read, and bump the TTL thresholds via extend_contract_instance_ttl / the appropriate storage bumps. See the Storage TTL / Rent pattern and the storage-ttl example for the threshold-bump pattern to copy. The same clock governs fees. A TTL bump has to be paid for; budgeting for rent is part of running a real token, not an afterthought. Security Considerations This is an unaudited example. The items below are the gaps it deliberately leaves open, not an exhaustive audit. Unrestricted Minting: The current implementation allows anyone to mint tokens. Add access control using an admin address or authorized minters list before production use. No Decimal Support: This basic implementation uses integers only. For real assets, consider implementing a decimals field and decimal-aware math. Supply Cap: Consider implementing a maximum supply to prevent unlimited inflation. Allowance/Approval: For more advanced use cases, implement an approve/transferFrom pattern allowing third parties to move tokens on behalf of the owner. The contract manages a ledger mapping addresses to token balances using persistent storage. Three public functions allow minting tokens, querying balances, and transferring between accounts. Unaudited teaching example The contract below is an unaudited educational example. It has not been through a security review and it is not fit for production or for holding real value — most obviously because mint is completely unrestricted, so anyone can inflate the supply at will. Read the two limits that matter most before you copy anything: Reentrancy — none of mint, balance, or transfer makes a cross-contract call, so there is no re-entrant call to defend against as written. The moment you add one (a transfer-fee hook, a mint callback, a cross-chain message), that protection is gone. See Reentrancy limits. Storage TTL / data expiry — balances live in persistent storage, which expires. This example never extends a TTL, so a balance can be archived and then permanently deleted, silently turning into a zero balance. See Reentrancy and storage TTL limits. For a real token, use the Stellar Asset Contract (SAC) or the SEP-41 standard instead of deploying this. Contract Running Tests #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contracterror, contractimpl, contracttype, Address, Env}; /// Storage key for tracking token balances per address. #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone)] pub enum DataKey { Balance(Address), } /// Error codes for token operations. #[contracterror] #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq, PartialOrd, Ord)] #[repr(u32)] pub enum Error { InsufficientBalance = 1, InvalidAmount = 2, SelfTransfer = 3, } #[contract] pub struct TokenTransfer; #[contractimpl] impl TokenTransfer { /// Mint tokens to an address (for testing and bootstrapping). /// In production, restrict this to authorized minters. pub fn mint(env: Env, to: Address, amount: i128) { let key = DataKey::Balance(to.clone()); let current: i128 = env.storage().persistent().get(&key).unwrap_or(0); env.storage().persistent().set(&key, &(current + amount)); } /// Query the token balance of an address. pub fn balance(env: Env, of: Address) -> i128 { let key = DataKey::Balance(of); env.storage().persistent().get(&key).unwrap_or(0) } /// Transfer tokens from sender to recipient. /// Requires authorization from the sender address. pub fn transfer(env: Env, from: Address, to: Address, amount: i128) -> Result<(), Error> { from.require_auth(); // Validate amount if amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } // Prevent self-transfer if from == to { return Err(Error::SelfTransfer); } // Check sender has sufficient balance let from_key = DataKey::Balance(from.clone()); let from_balance: i128 = env.storage().persistent().get(&from_key).unwrap_or(0); if from_balance < amount { return Err(Error::InsufficientBalance); } // Perform transfer let to_key = DataKey::Balance(to.clone()); let to_balance: i128 = env.storage().persistent().get(&to_key).unwrap_or(0); env.storage() .persistent() .set(&from_key, &(from_balance - amount)); env.storage() .persistent() .set(&to_key, &(to_balance + amount)); let client = TokenTransferClient::new(&env, &contract_id); (env, client) } #[test] fn test_mint_increases_balance() { let (env, client) = setup(); let alice = Address::generate(&env); client.mint(&alice, &500); assert_eq!(client.balance(&alice), 500); } #[test] fn test_transfer_moves_tokens() { let (env, client) = setup(); let alice = Address::generate(&env); let bob = Address::generate(&env); client.mint(&alice, &1000); client.transfer(&alice, &bob, &400); assert_eq!(client.balance(&alice), 600); assert_eq!(client.balance(&bob), 400); } #[test] fn test_transfer_fails_on_insufficient_balance() { let (env, client) = setup(); These two limits are the difference between a teaching contract and a token that can safely hold value. Neither is enforced by this example. Reentrancy limits​ Reentrancy does not apply as written, and that is the only reason. mint, balance, and transfer call env.storage() and nothing else — there is no cross-contract call, no token transfer, and no callback, so no external code ever regains control partway through a state update. Soroban runs an invocation to completion unless a contract deliberately calls into another contract. The guarantees you can rely on today, and what breaks them: transfer is checks-then-effects. It reads the sender balance, verifies from_balance >= amount, and only then writes both sides. That ordering is safe only because no untrusted code runs between the read and the write. Adding any external call breaks it. Insert a transfer-fee hook, a mint callback, a cross-chain invoke_contract, or a SAC payment between the read and the write and the pattern is exploitable: re-read both balances after the call, because the callee can move funds or change state in the meantime. to_balance is read before the write. That value can be stale if anything external ran in between. Re-read it after any external call. transfer does call from.require_auth() — that is an authorization check, not a reentrancy guard. It stops unauthorized senders; it does not stop a callee re-entering. Use the repo's guard shape. The Reentrancy Guard pattern sets a storage flag before any external work and clears it afterwards, so a re-entrant call panics rather than double-spending. Adopt it whenever you extend this contract. Storage TTL and data-expiry limits​ Balances are stored with env.storage().persistent(), and persistent entries expire. This is the single most dangerous omission in the example: Nothing here extends a TTL. There is no extend_ttl call anywhere in the contract, so each balance entry gets the network's default minimum lifetime and then starts counting down. Expiry is two-phase. When a persistent entry's TTL lapses, the ledger archives it: reads still succeed but return the archived (stale) value while restoration is pending. If it is not restored before the next ledger closes the retention window, the entry is deleted permanently. A deleted balance reads back as 0. Because balance uses .unwrap_or(0), permanent deletion is indistinguishable from "never had a balance". A holder's funds can vanish with no error and no event. Instance storage would not help. Instance entries expire with the contract instance, so a long-idle token loses everything at once. A production token must extend the TTL on every balance it touches, extend it for a minimum window ahead of expiry, restore archived entries on read, and bump the TTL thresholds via extend_contract_instance_ttl / the appropriate storage bumps. See the Storage TTL / Rent pattern and the storage-ttl example for the threshold-bump pattern to copy. The same clock governs fees. A TTL bump has to be paid for; budgeting for rent is part of running a real token, not an afterthought.

Batching combines similar operations into one contract invocation. The batch-ops example transfers one sender's balance to several recipients while requiring authorization only once and reading and writing the sender's balance only once. The example limits a batch to 20 operations. This is an application limit, not a Soroban protocol limit. Unaudited Example Code The example code in this pattern is for educational purposes and has not been audited for production use. Always conduct a thorough security audit before deploying to mainnet. When to batch Batch when operations share authorization or storage setup and callers benefit from fewer contract invocations. Prefer separate calls when operations need independent atomicity, unrelated authorization, or highly variable resource costs. Implementation Define one named limit and reject invalid batch sizes before changing state: pub const MAX_BATCH_SIZE: u32 = 20; pub fn batch_transfer( env: Env, from: Address, ops: Vec<TransferOp>, ) -> Result<Vec<OpResult>, Error> { from.require_auth(); if ops.is_empty() { return Err(Error::EmptyBatch); } if ops.len() > MAX_BATCH_SIZE { return Err(Error::BatchTooLarge); } let mut sender_balance = Self::balance_of(env.clone(), from.clone()); let mut results = Vec::new(&env); for op in ops.iter() { if op.amount <= 0 || sender_balance < op.amount { results.push_back(OpResult::InsufficientBalance); continue; } sender_balance -= op.amount; let recipient_balance = Self::balance_of(env.clone(), op.to.clone()); env.storage().persistent().set( &DataKey::Balance(op.to.clone()), &(recipient_balance + op.amount), ); results.push_back(OpResult::Ok); } env.storage() .persistent() .set(&DataKey::Balance(from), &sender_balance); Ok(results) } The loop is now predictable. Authorization and sender-balance storage costs are shared, while recipient reads and writes still grow linearly with successful operations. Boundary tests​ The test_batch_transfer_accepts_batch_at_exactly_the_limit test constructs exactly MAX_BATCH_SIZE operations and verifies that all 20 succeed. The companion over-limit test constructs 21 operations, expects Error::BatchTooLarge, and confirms that the sender's balance did not change. let mut ops = Vec::new(&env); for _ in 0..MAX_BATCH_SIZE { ops.push_back(TransferOp { to: Address::generate(&env), amount: 1, }); } let results = client.batch_transfer(&sender, &ops); assert_eq!(results.len(), MAX_BATCH_SIZE); A boundary test is not a budget measurement This proves the contract accepts 20 items; it does not prove every possible 20-item batch fits every network resource budget. Authorization, ledger footprint, contract changes, SDK upgrades, and network configuration can change the measured cost. Instruction and resource budget Soroban meters CPU instructions, memory, ledger reads and writes, event data, and transaction size. A caller-controlled loop consumes more of the transaction-wide budget for every item, including work performed by nested contract calls. Choose a production batch limit by measurement: Build optimized Wasm for the SDK and protocol version being deployed. Simulate sizes from 1 through the proposed maximum against realistic ledger state. Include a worst case: distinct recipients, successful writes, full authorization, and any downstream contract calls. Record CPU instructions, memory, ledger entries and bytes, transaction size, and resource fee. Set the application cap below the measured failure point, leaving upgrade and configuration margin. Repeat after upgrades and keep exact-limit and over-limit tests in CI. Do not derive MAX_BATCH_SIZE from a copied network instruction-limit number. Network limits are configuration, while the contract guard is part of its API and upgrade policy. See Gas and Resource Management for profiling guidance. Failure semantics EmptyBatch and BatchTooLarge reject the call before balance changes. A non-positive or overdrawing transfer returns OpResult::InsufficientBalance, is skipped, and does not stop later valid operations. Results preserve input order. A direct off-chain caller cannot undo successful items after the transaction commits. If a use case requires all-or-nothing behavior, validate every item before the first write or provide a separate atomic entry point. Security considerations Require the batch owner's authorization before processing any item. Run batch-level validation before writes or external calls. Cap every caller-controlled loop and include nested work in the estimate. Document ordering and partial-success semantics for clients. Decide whether duplicate recipients are valid; this example accumulates their transfers. This guide explains how the examples/constant-product-amm crate works, covering: The x·y=k invariant and its integer-arithmetic implementation Liquidity provision and proportional LP token minting Swap fee mechanics (0.3 %) with rounding Donation-attack mitigations Future work: fee collection (issue #185) Prerequisites Rust and cargo Soroban CLI and soroban_sdk Familiarity with token::Client and require_auth() Basic understanding of AMM design The x·y=k Invariant A constant-product AMM maintains the invariant: reserve_a × reserve_b = k where k is a constant that increases only when liquidity is added and decreases only when liquidity is removed. Every swap preserves k (minus a fee). Why integer arithmetic matters​ Soroban contracts use i128 for token amounts. Floating-point division does not exist. All arithmetic uses checked_mul / checked_div to: Prevent overflow (returns Error::Overflow instead of wrapping). Accept rounding-down in the swapper's favor — the pool always keeps ≥ the theoretical share. Swap output formula​ For a swap of amount_in of token A for token B, the output is: amount_out = (amount_in_with_fee × reserve_b) / (reserve_a × 1000 + amount_in_with_fee) where amount_in_with_fee = amount_in × 997 (applying the 0.3 % fee by working in thousandths). The same formula applies symmetrically for B→A swaps. Rounding and Precision All division in this crate uses integer truncation (floor division). This means: Swappers receive slightly less than the theoretical output — this is intentional and keeps the pool solvent. LP minting (via sqrt for the initial deposit) also truncates, slightly under-counting the first LP's share. amount_a_min / amount_b_min slippage guards protect swappers from unacceptable rounding. Tip: For production deployments with very small token denominations (e.g., 7-decimal Stellar assets with tiny amounts), verify that rounding does not produce 0-output swaps. The crate returns Error::InsufficientOutput if amount_out ≤ 0. Donation-Attack Mitigations A donation attack occurs when a malicious actor transfers tokens directly to the contract address (bypassing the pool's swap logic), artificially inflating one reserve relative to the other without updating storage. This can: Break the invariant check. Allow the attacker to drain value from LPs by removing liquidity at the inflated ratio. How this crate mitigates donations: The crate tracks reserves exclusively in env.storage().persistent() under DataKey::Reserves. Reserve values are only updated through add_liquidity, remove_liquidity, swap_a_for_b, and swap_b_for_a. The contract never re-reads reserves from token balances; therefore, direct token transfers to the contract address do not affect the stored invariant. Note: This is a storage-based mitigation. If you add an on-chain balance sync function (e.g., sync_reserves), you must ensure it is properly access-controlled to avoid griefing. This sets the initial price and anchors the invariant. Removing liquidity​ pub fn remove_liquidity( env: Env, caller: Address, lp_amount: i128, amount_a_min: i128, amount_b_min: i128, ) -> Result<(i128, i128), Error> { caller.require_auth(); // amount_a = lp_amount × reserve_a / lp_total_supply // amount_b = lp_amount × reserve_b / lp_total_supply } Swap A → B​ pub fn swap_a_for_b( env: Env, caller: Address, amount_a_in: i128, min_b_out: i128, ) -> Result<i128, Error> { caller.require_auth(); let amount_a_in_with_fee = amount_a_in.checked_mul(997).ok_or(Error::Overflow)?; let numerator = amount_a_in_with_fee.checked_mul(reserves.reserve_b).ok_or(Error::Overflow)?; let denominator = reserves.reserve_a.checked_mul(1000).ok_or(Error::Overflow)? .checked_add(amount_a_in_with_fee).ok_or(Error::Overflow)?; let amount_b_out = numerator.checked_div(denominator).ok_or(Error::Overflow)?; if amount_b_out < min_b_out { return Err(Error::InsufficientOutput); } // Transfer tokens; update stored reserves } The symmetric swap_b_for_a applies the same formula with roles reversed. // From examples/constant-product-amm/test_snapshots/tests // Run: cargo test -p constant-product-amm #[test] fn test_swap_a_for_b() { // ... set up env, register tokens, add liquidity, then: let out = client.swap_a_for_b(&caller, &1_000_000i128, &0i128); assert!(out > 0); } #[test] fn test_insufficient_output_slippage() { // Expect InsufficientOutput when min_b_out is too high } #[test] fn test_add_remove_liquidity_roundtrip() { // LP should receive close to deposited amounts after remove } Run the full suite: cd examples/constant-product-amm cargo test Future work: fees (issue #185) The current 0.3 % fee is burned into the swap math but not collected separately. A constant-product AMM maintains the invariant: reserve_a × reserve_b = k where k is a constant that increases only when liquidity is added and decreases only when liquidity is removed. Every swap preserves k (minus a fee). Why integer arithmetic matters​ Soroban contracts use i128 for token amounts. Floating-point division does not exist. All arithmetic uses checked_mul / checked_div to: Prevent overflow (returns Error::Overflow instead of wrapping). Accept rounding-down in the swapper's favor — the pool always keeps ≥ the theoretical share. Swap output formula​ For a swap of amount_in of token A for token B, the output is: amount_out = (amount_in_with_fee × reserve_b) / (reserve_a × 1000 + amount_in_with_fee) where amount_in_with_fee = amount_in × 997 (applying the 0.3 % fee by working in thousandths). The same formula applies symmetrically for B→A swaps.

Soroban contracts use i128 for token amounts. Floating-point division does not exist. All arithmetic uses checked_mul / checked_div to: Prevent overflow (returns Error::Overflow instead of wrapping). Accept rounding-down in the swapper's favor — the pool always keeps ≥ the theoretical share.

For a swap of amount_in of token A for token B, the output is: amount_out = (amount_in_with_fee × reserve_b) / (reserve_a × 1000 + amount_in_with_fee) where amount_in_with_fee = amount_in × 997 (applying the 0.3 % fee by working in thousandths). The same formula applies symmetrically for B→A swaps.

All division in this crate uses integer truncation (floor division). This means: Swappers receive slightly less than the theoretical output — this is intentional and keeps the pool solvent. LP minting (via sqrt for the initial deposit) also truncates, slightly under-counting the first LP's share. amount_a_min / amount_b_min slippage guards protect swappers from unacceptable rounding. Tip: For production deployments with very small token denominations (e.g., 7-decimal Stellar assets with tiny amounts), verify that rounding does not produce 0-output swaps. The crate returns Error::InsufficientOutput if amount_out ≤ 0.

A donation attack occurs when a malicious actor transfers tokens directly to the contract address (bypassing the pool's swap logic), artificially inflating one reserve relative to the other without updating storage. This can: Break the invariant check. Allow the attacker to drain value from LPs by removing liquidity at the inflated ratio. How this crate mitigates donations: The crate tracks reserves exclusively in env.storage().persistent() under DataKey::Reserves. Reserve values are only updated through add_liquidity, remove_liquidity, swap_a_for_b, and swap_b_for_a. The contract never re-reads reserves from token balances; therefore, direct token transfers to the contract address do not affect the stored invariant. Note: This is a storage-based mitigation. If you add an on-chain balance sync function (e.g., sync_reserves), you must ensure it is properly access-controlled to avoid griefing.

This sets the initial price and anchors the invariant.

pub fn remove_liquidity( env: Env, caller: Address, lp_amount: i128, amount_a_min: i128, amount_b_min: i128, ) -> Result<(i128, i128), Error> { caller.require_auth(); // amount_a = lp_amount × reserve_a / lp_total_supply // amount_b = lp_amount × reserve_b / lp_total_supply }

pub fn swap_a_for_b( env: Env, caller: Address, amount_a_in: i128, min_b_out: i128, ) -> Result<i128, Error> { caller.require_auth(); let amount_a_in_with_fee = amount_a_in.checked_mul(997).ok_or(Error::Overflow)?; let numerator = amount_a_in_with_fee.checked_mul(reserves.reserve_b).ok_or(Error::Overflow)?; let denominator = reserves.reserve_a.checked_mul(1000).ok_or(Error::Overflow)? .checked_add(amount_a_in_with_fee).ok_or(Error::Overflow)?; let amount_b_out = numerator.checked_div(denominator).ok_or(Error::Overflow)?; if amount_b_out < min_b_out { return Err(Error::InsufficientOutput); } // Transfer tokens; update stored reserves } The symmetric swap_b_for_a applies the same formula with roles reversed.

The current 0.3 % fee is burned into the swap math but not collected separately. Issue #185 tracks adding a fee collection mechanism: A dedicated fee_recipient address accumulates a portion of each swap fee. LP holders receive the remainder as increased reserve value on removal. Until #185 is resolved, the entire fee accrues proportionally to LP holders through reserve appreciation.

No slippage protection — always pass non-zero min_b_out / amount_a_min / amount_b_min in production clients. The contract factory pattern enables dynamic deployment of multiple contract instances from a single factory contract. This is useful for creating standardized contracts at runtime without manual deployment.

A factory contract acts as a centralized deployer that can: Deploy child contract instances on-demand Track all deployed instances Initialize child contracts with custom parameters Manage the lifecycle of multiple contracts

Token Issuance: Deploy a new token contract for each asset User Accounts: Create individual contract instances for user-specific logic Multi-tenancy: Deploy isolated instances for different organizations Pool Management: Create liquidity pools dynamically Marketplace: Deploy individual shop contracts from a marketplace factory

The factory pattern typically consists of: Factory Contract: Manages deployment and tracking Child Contract: The template contract that gets deployed multiple times Registry: Maintains a list of deployed instances Factory Contract ├── deploy_child(name) ├── get_deployed_children() └── child_count() Child Contract (Template) ├── init(name) ├── get_name() └── get_info()

Unaudited learning example This factory pattern is unaudited teaching material and is not production-ready. Do not deploy it with real funds, authority over child contracts, or production registries without a full security review and tests for your deployment, initialization, and access-control rules. The snippets do not demonstrate reentrancy protection. Factory deployments and child initialization can involve cross-contract behavior in real systems, so production code should update factory state in a deliberate order, prevent duplicate initialization, and treat child calls as external interactions that may fail or invoke unexpected code paths.

The child contract is the template that will be deployed multiple times: #[contract] pub struct ChildContract; #[contractimpl] impl ChildContract { pub fn init(env: Env, name: Symbol) { env.storage().instance().set(&symbol_short!("name"), &name); } pub fn get_name(env: Env) -> Symbol { env.storage() .instance() .get(&symbol_short!("name")) .unwrap_or(Symbol::new(&env, "unnamed")) } pub fn get_info(env: Env) -> (Symbol, Address) { let name = env .storage() .instance() .get(&symbol_short!("name")) .unwrap_or(Symbol::new(&env, "unnamed")); let contract_id = env.current_contract_address(); (name, contract_id) } }

The factory deploys and tracks child instances: #[contract] pub struct ContractFactory; #[contractimpl] impl ContractFactory { pub fn deploy_child(env: Env, name: Symbol) -> Address { // Get child contract code let child_code = env.deployer().get_programm_id(&symbol_short!("child")); // Generate unique salt for deterministic deployment let salt = env.storage().temporary().get::<(), u64>(&()).unwrap_or(0); env.storage() .temporary() .set(&(), &(salt + 1)); let salt_bytes = salt.to_le_bytes().to_vec(); // Deploy new instance let child_address = env .deployer() .deploy_contract( &salt_bytes, &child_code, Address::from_contract_id(&env.current_contract_address()) ); // Track deployed contract let mut deployed: Vec<Address> = env .storage() .persistent() .get(&symbol_short!("deployed")) .unwrap_or_else(|| vec![&env]); deployed.push_back(child_address.clone()); env.storage() .persistent() .set(&symbol_short!("deployed"), &deployed); child_address } pub fn get_deployed_children(env: Env) -> Vec<Address> { env.storage() .persistent() .get(&symbol_short!("deployed")) .unwrap_or_else(|| vec![&env]) } pub fn child_count(env: Env) -> u32 { let deployed: Vec<Address> = env .storage() .persistent() .get(&symbol_short!("deployed")) .unwrap_or_else(|| vec![&env]); deployed.len() as u32 } }

The factory pattern includes comprehensive tests: #[test] fn test_factory_deploy_multiple_children() { let env = Env::default(); let factory_contract_id = env.register_contract(None, ContractFactory); let factory_client = ContractFactoryClient::new(&env, &factory_contract_id); // Deploy multiple children let child1 = factory_client.deploy_child(&Symbol::new(&env, "child-1")); let child2 = factory_client.deploy_child(&Symbol::new(&env, "child-2")); let child3 = factory_client.deploy_child(&Symbol::new(&env, "child-3")); // Verify all are tracked assert_eq!(factory_client.child_count(), 3); let deployed = factory_client.get_deployed_children(); assert_eq!(deployed.len(), 3); assert!(deployed.contains(&child1)); assert!(deployed.contains(&child2)); assert!(deployed.contains(&child3)); }

Use unique salts to ensure different deployment addresses: let salt = env.storage().temporary().get::<(), u64>(&()).unwrap_or(0); let salt_bytes = salt.to_le_bytes().to_vec(); The salt, combined with the factory's own address, is what determines each child's contract ID — see Contract IDs & Deploy Salt for how that derivation works and how to predict a child's address before deploying it.
Persistent storage: For tracking important metadata Temporary storage: For non-critical counters Instance storage: For child contract-specific data
Always initialize child contracts with necessary parameters: client.init(&name);
Maintain a registry of deployed instances for: Verification Monitoring Upgrade coordination Access control

Pass parameters when deploying: pub fn deploy_child_with_params( env: Env, name: Symbol, owner: Address, config: Config, ) -> Address { // Deploy let child_address = /* deployment logic */; // Initialize with parameters let client = ChildContractClient::new(&env, &child_address); client.init(&name); // ... set owner, config, etc child_address }

Restrict who can deploy: pub fn deploy_child(env: Env, name: Symbol) -> Address { let caller = env.invoker(); let authorized: Address = env.storage() .persistent() .get(&symbol_short!("admin")) .expect("Admin not set"); require_auth(&caller); require!(caller == authorized, Error::NotAuthorized); // Deploy logic... }

Retrieve specific child contracts: pub fn get_child_by_index(env: Env, index: u32) -> Address { let deployed: Vec<Address> = env .storage() .persistent() .get(&symbol_short!("deployed")) .unwrap_or_else(|| vec![&env]); deployed.get(index as usize) }

Unique Salts: Ensure each deployment uses a unique salt Initialization: Always initialize child contracts properly Tracking: Maintain a registry of deployed instances Access Control: Restrict deployment permissions if needed Testing: Test deployment, tracking, and retrieval Documentation: Document child contract interfaces clearly

A contract registry provides a stable name-to-address mapping for deployed contracts. This is useful alongside a contract factory: the factory deploys new contract instances, and the registry provides a stable name so clients do not need to track raw contract addresses.

The registry contract allows an administrator to: Set a name-to-address mapping Get the address for a registered name Update existing mappings (overwrite) Only the authorized administrator can update entries. All addresses can read mappings.

Service Discovery: Map human-readable names to contract addresses Factory Integration: Register contracts deployed by a factory Version Management: Point a name to the latest contract version Multi-contract Systems: Provide stable references across contract upgrades
Registry Contract ├── initialize(admin) ├── set(name, address) ├── get(name) -> Option<Address> └── admin() -> Option<Address>
Names are Bytes objects between 1 and 32 bytes. This supports: ASCII strings: b"token", b"vault" Hex-encoded identifiers: b"0x1234" Binary keys (for programmatic use)

Unaudited Educational Example — Not for Production This contract pattern is an educational example and has not undergone an independent security audit. Do not deploy this snippet to production or mainnet without substantial hardening, complete test coverage, and formal review. Security & Architectural Limitations: Reentrancy: The current implementation performs simple instance storage reads and writes without external cross-contract invocations or token transfers, meaning external reentrancy vectors do not directly apply. However, if external calls or callbacks are added in future extensions, proper checks-effects-interactions order or a reentrancy guard must be implemented. Storage TTL & Data Expiry: All administrative configuration and registry entries reside in instance storage. Instance storage entries share the contract instance's time-to-live (TTL). If the instance TTL is not routinely monitored and extended via env.storage().instance().extend_ttl(...), entries will expire and become inaccessible, rendering the name service unavailable until restored.

pub fn set(env: Env, name: Bytes, address: Address) -> Result<(), Error> { let admin: Address = env .storage() .instance() .get(&DataKey::Admin) .ok_or(Error::NotInitialized)?; admin.require_auth(); if name.len() == 0 || name.len() > 32 { return Err(Error::NameTooLong); } env.storage() .instance() .set(&DataKey::Entry(name), &address); Ok(()) } pub fn get(env: Env, name: Bytes) -> Option<Address> { env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::Entry(name)) }

Authorization: Only the admin can call set Overwrite: Calling set on an existing name updates the address Missing entries: get returns None for unregistered names Name validation: Names must be 1–32 bytes

The implementation includes comprehensive tests: #[test] fn set_and_get_registered_name() { let fixture = setup(); initialize(&fixture); let n = name(&fixture.env, "my-contract"); let addr = Address::generate(&fixture.env); fixture.client.set(&n, &addr); assert_eq!(fixture.client.get(&n), Some(addr)); } #[test] fn unauthorized_set_fails() { let env = Env::default(); let admin = Address::generate(&env); let unauthorized = Address::generate(&env); let contract_id = env.register(Registry, ()); let client = RegistryClient::new(&env, &contract_id); env.mock_auths(&[MockAuth { ... }]); client.initialize(&admin); let n = name(&env, "my-contract"); let addr = Address::generate(&env); // Try with unauthorized address env.mock_auths(&[MockAuth { ... }]); let result = client.try_set(&n, &addr); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::Unauthorized))); }

Registry initialization with admin Authorized set() and get() roundtrip Update existing name overwrites address Unauthorized set() fails Multiple names map to different contracts Missing name returns None Empty name rejected Name over 32 bytes rejected Reinitialization rejected

The registry pairs naturally with the Contract Factory pattern: Factory: deploy_child(name) -> address Registry: set(name, address) Factory deploys a new contract and returns its address The address is registered under a stable name Clients resolve the name to get the current address This separation allows: Upgrades: Deploy a new contract and update the registry entry Discovery: Clients look up contracts by name, not address Governance: Registry updates can require multi-sig approval

A minimal contract that stores a single integer counter in instance storage. It demonstrates the three core storage operations — read, write, and reset — and serves as the reference example for the snippet-drift convention introduced in Phase 8 (issue #644).

Every Rust fence that carries a src= attribute in its info string is treated as a direct copy of the referenced file under examples/. CI runs scripts/check-snippet-drift.sh to verify that the snippet has not drifted from its source. If the two differ, the check fails and the PR is blocked. ```rust src=counter/src/lib.rs The path is always relative to the examples/ directory.

Unaudited teaching example The contract below is an unaudited educational example, published so the core instance-storage operations stay easy to read. It has not been through a security review and it is not fit for production or real value. Copying it verbatim is fine for learning; deploying it as-is with funds at risk is not. Before any production use, add the missing access control, run a full audit, and re-derive the storage and overflow behaviour for your own use case. The Security considerations section lists what this example deliberately leaves out. counter/src/lib.rs Cargo.toml // SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT // Copyright (c) 2026 Soroban Cookbook #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, Env}; const COUNTER_KEY: &str = "count"; #[contract] pub struct Counter; #[contractimpl] impl Counter { /// Increment the counter by one and return the new value. pub fn increment(env: Env) -> u32 { let count: u32 = env.storage().instance().get(&COUNTER_KEY).unwrap_or(0); let new_count = count + 1; env.storage().instance().set(&COUNTER_KEY, &new_count); new_count } /// Return the current counter value without modifying state. pub fn get(env: Env) -> u32 { env.storage().instance().get(&COUNTER_KEY).unwrap_or(0) } /// Reset the counter to zero. pub fn reset(env: Env) { env.storage().instance().set(&COUNTER_KEY, &0_u32); } } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; use soroban_sdk::Env; #[test] fn test_initial_value_is_zero() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register(Counter, ()); let client = CounterClient::new(&env, &contract_id); assert_eq!(client.get(), 0); } #[test] fn test_increment_increases_count() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register(Counter, ()); let client = CounterClient::new(&env, &contract_id); assert_eq!(client.increment(), 1); assert_eq!(client.increment(), 2); assert_eq!(client.increment(), 3); } #[test] fn test_reset_returns_to_zero() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register(Counter, ()); let client = CounterClient::new(&env, &contract_id); client.increment(); client.increment(); assert_eq!(client.get(), 2); client.reset(); assert_eq!(client.get(), 0); } #[test] fn test_get_does_not_change_state() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register(Counter, ()); let client = CounterClient::new(&env, &contract_id); client.increment(); assert_eq!(client.get(), 1); assert_eq!(client.get(), 1); } } [package] name = "counter" version = "0.1.0" edition = "2021" [lib] crate-type = ["cdylib", "rlib"] [dependencies] soroban-sdk = { version = "27.0.3", features = ["testutils"] } [dev-dependencies] soroban-sdk = { version = "27.0.3", features = ["testutils"] } [profile.release] opt-level = "z" overflow-checks = true debug = 0 strip = "symbols" debug-assertions = false panic = "abort" codegen-units = 1 lto = true

instance storage ties the lifetime of entries to the contract instance itself. An entry is evicted from the ledger when the instance's TTL expires and is not extended. For a simple counter that is called frequently this is the right choice — every invocation naturally extends the TTL.

Using a compile-time &str constant (COUNTER_KEY) rather than an enum variant keeps the example minimal. For contracts with many keys, prefer a #[contracttype] enum so the Soroban SDK can derive serialisation.

Unaudited example This pattern is an unaudited teaching example. It is not fit for production use with real value, and the gaps below are intentional — they keep the storage mechanics visible. Close them, and get a security review, before you deploy anything derived from it. No access control is applied. Any account can increment, read, or reset the counter. Add require_auth if you need to restrict who can mutate state. u32 wraps at 4 294 967 295; overflow-checks = true in the release profile causes the process to abort on overflow in debug builds. In production, add explicit bounds checking if overflow is a concern.

Not applicable as written, and that is the point. None of increment, get, or reset makes a cross-contract call, and none of them transfer value, so there is no reentrant call to defend against. Soroban also executes a single invocation to completion unless a contract deliberately calls into another contract, which this one never does. The moment you extend this pattern, the reasoning stops applying. Concretely: If you add a hook or callback (an oracle push, a reward payout, a transfer of some minted asset), the callee gets control back in the middle of your function. Re-read every value you are about to write after the call, or the callee can hand you a stale balance. reset is the dangerous one. It writes 0 to the single key COUNTER_KEY with no authorization. Paired with any external call added to the same function, it becomes a trivial griefing vector — anyone can zero the counter mid-operation. Prefer the guard the repo already ships. The Reentrancy Guard pattern sets a storage flag before external work and clears it after, so a re-entrant call panics instead of corrupting state. Copy that shape rather than hand-rolling a check. get is safe to call from anywhere. It only reads, so it is fine to expose as a cross-contract entry point. In short: this example is reentrancy-free because it is reentrancy-trivial. Keep it that way, or adopt the guard pattern when you extend it.

This pattern demonstrates a small but realistic Soroban layout where a vault contract calls an external token contract. The example is deliberately split into multiple crates/modules so the roles are clear: the token contract owns balances and authorization the vault contract owns accounting and cross-contract orchestration the test module exercises the full call chain end-to-end

Use this pattern when a contract depends on another deployed contract for: balance checks and transfers price or data feeds access control checks delegated to a trusted service multi-contract workflows that must remain atomic in a single transaction This is the same shape used in real DeFi systems: caller contract, callee contract, and explicit failure handling at each boundary. Unaudited Example Code The example code in this pattern is for educational purposes and has not been audited for production use. Always conduct a thorough security audit before deploying to mainnet.

examples/cross-contract/ ├── Cargo.toml ├── README.md ├── src/ │ ├── lib.rs # exposes Token and Vault modules │ ├── token.rs # callee: balance logic + require_auth │ ├── vault.rs # caller: typed client + try_* fallback handling │ ├── test.rs # end-to-end deployment and auth assertions │ └── main.rs # demo entry point for the example crate └── target/ # generated by cargo test

File Role Why it matters src/token.rs Callee contract Tracks balances and requires require_auth() before transfer or mint flows. src/vault.rs Caller contract Stores a configured token contract address and invokes TokenClient methods. src/test.rs Integration tests Deploys both contracts in the same Env, then verifies deposit, withdrawal, auth, and rollback behavior. src/lib.rs Module wiring Re-exports the contracts so the tests and the example crate can import them cleanly.
The important pattern is that the callee enforces authorization while the caller enforces the business workflow around that external dependency.

The vault uses the generated client from the token contract: let token_client = TokenClient::new(&env, &token_contract); match token_client.try_transfer(&from, &env.current_contract_address(), &amount) { Ok(Ok(())) => { /* success */ } Ok(Err(_)) | Err(_) => { /* safe fallback */ } } This gives compile-time verification of the token interface while still allowing recovery from host-level or contract-level failures.
The vault updates its local ledger state before it invokes the token transfer. That keeps the business accounting consistent even if the external call fails and the transaction is rolled back.
Where a contract failure is recoverable, the vault uses try_transfer and try_risky_operation instead of allowing an unhandled panic to abort the entire transaction.
The token requires the sender to authorize transfers, and the vault only calls the token after the user or admin has been validated by the surrounding workflow.

From the repository root: cargo test --manifest-path examples/cross-contract/Cargo.toml Or run inside the example directory: cd examples/cross-contract cargo test The test suite covers: successful deposit and withdrawal flows insufficient balance failures emergency mode and admin authorization checks token validation on initialization / update rollback behavior when a callee call fails

#[test] fn test_successful_deposit_and_withdrawal() { let (env, _token_id, token_client, _vault_id, vault_client, admin) = setup_contracts(); let user = Address::generate(&env); token_client.mint(&user, &1000i128).unwrap(); vault_client.deposit(&user, &1000i128).unwrap(); assert_eq!(vault_client.user_balance(&user), 1000); vault_client.withdraw(&user, &300i128).unwrap(); assert_eq!(vault_client.user_balance(&user), 700); } The tests use the Soroban Env sandbox, register both contracts, and assert on the exact state transitions that would occur in production.

In Soroban, types are more than just data containers—they define the contract's storage footprint, gas efficiency, and long-term maintainability. This guide covers strategies for designing custom types that are robust, efficient, and evolvable. Why Type Design Matters Smart contracts are immutable by nature, but their state persists across upgrades. Poorly designed types can lead to "storage bloat," high gas costs for reads/writes, and complex migrations when business requirements change. ⚠️ Unaudited Examples — Not for Production All code snippets on this page are educational examples only. They have not been audited and must not be deployed with real funds or in any production environment without a thorough independent security review. Reentrancy: Soroban's execution model does not support in-contract reentrancy — a contract cannot call back into itself mid-execution. However, cross-contract calls can introduce reentrancy-like vulnerabilities if storage reads and writes are not ordered carefully. Always write state changes before making outgoing cross-contract calls (checks-effects-interactions pattern). Storage TTL / Data Expiry: Soroban uses a rent-based storage model. Entries in persistent() storage expire after their TTL (time-to-live) ledger unless the rent is extended. instance() storage shares the contract's own TTL. temporary() storage is short-lived by design. If a TTL lapses, the ledger entry is archived and reads will fail. Any production contract that stores custom types must call env.storage().persistent().extend_ttl(...) (or the appropriate variant) to keep entries live. The patterns below do not include TTL extension calls — add them before deploying to Testnet or Mainnet.
When translating domain concepts (like "User Account" or "Liquidity Pool") into contract types, you must decide how to represent them in storage.

Value Objects: Types defined by their attributes (e.g., Amount, Price). In Soroban, these are usually small structs or newtype wrappers. Entities: Types with a unique identity that persists over time (e.g., User, Proposal). These are typically stored as large structs keyed by a unique ID or Address.

Use the "Newtype" pattern to wrap primitive types. This prevents accidental confusion between different units or IDs that share the same underlying type. #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub struct OrderId(pub u32); #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub struct TokenId(pub u32); // Compiler will prevent passing a TokenId where an OrderId is expected pub fn get_order(env: Env, id: OrderId) { ... }
Soroban uses a highly optimized serialization format (XDR). To make a custom type usable in a contract, it must be annotated with #[contracttype].

Structs: For grouping related data. Enums: For representing state or mutually exclusive options. Prims: i128, u32, Address, Bytes, Symbol, etc. #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub enum ContractState { Active, Paused, Upgrading(u32), // Enums can carry data } #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub struct Order { pub id: OrderId, pub owner: Address, pub amount: i128, pub status: ContractState, }
Every byte stored in the ledger costs gas. Serialization size directly impacts the read_ledger_entry and write_ledger_entry costs.

Prefer Small Primitives: Use u32 or u64 instead of i128 if the value range allows. Avoid Unnecessary Strings: Use Symbol for short, fixed strings (up to 32 characters). They are significantly cheaper than String. Flat vs. Nested: Highly nested structs increase serialization complexity. Keep storage types as flat as possible. Bit-Packing (Advanced): For extremely high-frequency operations, consider packing multiple booleans or small integers into a single u64. Read/Write Amplification Reading a 1KB struct to change a single boolean field still costs the gas for a 1KB read. If a struct grows too large, consider splitting it into separate storage keys.

Use enums to manage the lifecycle of a contract or entity. This makes illegal transitions impossible at the type level. #[contracttype] pub enum ProposalStatus { Pending, Voting { start_time: u64, end_time: u64 }, Executed, Expired, } pub fn cast_vote(env: Env, id: u32) -> Result<(), Error> { let proposal = get_proposal(&env, id)?; match proposal.status { ProposalStatus::Voting { start_time, end_time } => { let now = env.ledger().timestamp(); if now < start_time || now > end_time { return Err(Error::VotingNotActive); } // Proceed with voting... } _ => return Err(Error::InvalidStatus), } Ok(()) }

Group global contract settings into a single struct. This is more efficient than storing 10 separate configuration variables in 10 different storage keys. #[contracttype] pub struct Config { pub admin: Address, pub fee_bps: u32, pub min_deposit: i128, } impl Config { pub fn get(env: &Env) -> Self { env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::Config).unwrap() } }
Never trust data coming into the contract. Validate types at the entry point (contractimpl).

Range Checks: Ensure amounts are positive and within expected bounds. Sanitization: Check that Address types aren't the null address if applicable. State Invariants: Verify that the internal state of a struct is consistent (e.g., start_time < end_time). pub fn create_order(env: Env, amount: i128) -> Result<(), Error> { if amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } // ... }
As your project grows, you may need to add fields to your structs. Because storage is persistent, you must handle "schema drift."

Instead of storing a raw struct, store an enum that wraps different versions of the data. #[contracttype] pub enum AccountState { V1(AccountV1), V2(AccountV2), } #[contracttype] pub struct AccountV1 { pub balance: i128, } #[contracttype] pub struct AccountV2 { pub balance: i128, pub rewards_points: u64, // New field added in V2 } // Lazy Migration pub fn get_account(env: &Env, user: Address) -> AccountV2 { let state: AccountState = env.storage().persistent().get(&user).unwrap(); match state { AccountState::V1(v1) => { // Upgrade V1 to V2 on the fly AccountV2 { balance: v1.balance, rewards_points: 0, } } AccountState::V2(v2) => v2, } }

Integer Overflows: Always use checked math (checked_add, checked_mul) when performing calculations on numeric types. Unbounded Collections: Avoid using Vec or Map in storage types if they can grow indefinitely. This can lead to "gas exhaustion" attacks where reading the state becomes impossible. Type Confusion: Use Symbol or OrderId wrappers to ensure you aren't using a user-provided integer to index into the wrong data structure.

All custom types are annotated with #[contracttype]. Enums are used to represent state and avoid "boolean soup." Newtype wrappers protect against ID/unit confusion. Large structs are evaluated for potential splitting to save gas. A migration strategy (like Versioned State) is planned for future updates. Inputs are validated at the contract boundary.
You can find a complete end‑to‑end example in the examples/custom-types directory.

This pattern guide defines a comprehensive error handling methodology for Soroban smart contracts. It covers establishing a clear error taxonomy, implementing custom error patterns, executing propagation strategies, and ensuring user-facing clarity. Unaudited Examples — Not for Production All code snippets on this page are educational examples only. They have not been audited and must not be deployed with real funds or in any production environment without a thorough independent security review. Reentrancy: Soroban's execution model does not permit a contract to call back into itself mid-execution. However, cross-contract calls can still introduce reentrancy-like hazards if state writes are deferred until after an outgoing call. Apply the checks-effects-interactions pattern: validate inputs and update state before making any cross-contract call, and return errors from that updated state rather than from pre-call reads. Storage TTL / Data Expiry: Soroban uses a ledger-rent model. Entries in persistent() storage expire after their TTL unless rent is extended via extend_ttl. instance() storage expires with the contract itself; temporary() storage is intentionally short-lived. If an entry expires, reads return None (or panic on unwrap()), which will surface as unexpected NotInitialized or similar errors at runtime. Production contracts must manage TTL extension explicitly. The examples below omit TTL extension calls for brevity — add them before deploying to Testnet or Mainnet. Prerequisites Rust stable and cargo Soroban CLI installed Basic understanding of Rust's Result type and enum definitions Familiarity with the soroban_sdk environment Error Taxonomy and Custom Patterns A well-defined error taxonomy categorizes errors into logical groups. This prevents overlapping error codes, aids debugging, and makes client-side handling predictable. Common Taxonomy Categories​ Validation Errors (100-199): Invalid inputs, out of bounds, incorrect formats. Authorization Errors (200-299): Missing signatures, unauthorized roles. State Errors (300-399): Invalid state transitions, uninitialized data. Resource Errors (400-499): Insufficient balance, out of gas. Contract Test #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, contracttype, Env, Address}; #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub enum Error { // Validation Errors (100+) InvalidAmount = 101, InvalidAddress = 102, // Authorization Errors (200+) Unauthorized = 201, RoleNotFound = 202, // State Errors (300+) AlreadyInitialized = 301, NotInitialized = 302, // Resource Errors (400+) InsufficientBalance = 401, InsufficientAllowance = 402, } #[contract] pub struct TokenContract; #[contractimpl] impl TokenContract { pub fn transfer( env: Env, from: Address, to: Address, amount: i128, ) -> Result<(), Error> { from.require_auth(); if amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } let balance = env.storage().persistent().get(&from).unwrap_or(0); if balance < amount { return Err(Error::InsufficientBalance); } // Execute transfer logic here (simplified for example) let new_balance = balance - amount; env.storage().persistent().set(&from, &new_balance); Ok(()) } } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; use soroban_sdk::{testutils::Address as _, Env}; #[test] fn test_taxonomy_errors() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register_contract(None, TokenContract); let client = TokenContractClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let alice = Address::generate(&env); let bob = Address::generate(&env); env.mock_all_auths(); // Test Validation Error (100-199 range) let result = client.try_transfer(&alice, &bob, &-10); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::InvalidAmount))); // Test Resource Error (400-499 range) let result = client.try_transfer(&alice, &bob, &100); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::InsufficientBalance))); } } Decision Tree Before choosing an error strategy, review the Error Handling concept decision tree for when to return Result, use panic!, or use panic_with_error!. Propagation and Handling Strategies Using the ? operator allows you to gracefully propagate errors up the call stack. This pattern advocates breaking complex operations into smaller, isolated functions that validate conditions or calculate state and return a Result. Why Propagate? Propagating errors rather than panicking ensures that your contract gracefully halts and provides exact error reasons to the caller, preventing unknown execution states. Contract Test #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, Env, Address}; #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub enum WorkflowError { InvalidInput = 1, ProcessingFailed = 2, } #[contract] pub struct WorkflowContract; #[contractimpl] impl WorkflowContract { pub fn complex_workflow(env: Env, user: Address, value: i128) -> Result<(), WorkflowError> { user.require_auth(); // Strategy: Delegate and propagate errors using '?' Self::validate_input(&env, value)?; Self::process_data(&env, &user, value)?; Ok(()) } fn validate_input(_env: &Env, value: i128) -> Result<(), WorkflowError> { if value < 0 { return Err(WorkflowError::InvalidInput); } Ok(()) } fn process_data(env: &Env, user: &Address, value: i128) -> Result<(), WorkflowError> { // Business logic that could fail if value == 42 { return Err(WorkflowError::ProcessingFailed); } env.storage().persistent().set(user, &value); Ok(()) } } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; use soroban_sdk::{testutils::Address as _, Env}; #[test] fn test_error_propagation() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register_contract(None, WorkflowContract); let client = WorkflowContractClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let user = Address::generate(&env); env.mock_all_auths(); // The error naturally propagates from validate_input up to the contract entrypoint let result_validation = client.try_complex_workflow(&user, &-5); assert_eq!(result_validation, Err(Ok(WorkflowError::InvalidInput))); // The error propagates from process_data up to the contract entrypoint let result_processing = client.try_complex_workflow(&user, &42); assert_eq!(result_processing, Err(Ok(WorkflowError::ProcessingFailed))); } } User-Facing Clarity Recommendations To ensure frontend clients and indexers can clearly interpret contract failures, implement these recommendations: Standardize Error Codes: Publicly document your error taxonomy in your repository (e.g., in a README or developer portal). Clients rely on these numerical codes. Emit Telemetry Events: For critical path failures, emit an event before returning an error. This aids indexing services in tracking exact failure reasons. Use Descriptive Enums: Naming your Rust enum variants clearly translates to easier debugging when using the Soroban CLI or SDK tools. Provide Client-Side Mapping: Create an SDK or frontend utility mapping the numeric u32 error codes to human-readable messages (e.g., 101 -> "The requested token amount is invalid"). Event Emission on Failure Remember that if a contract returns an error, the transaction rolls back, and any events emitted during that invocation are dropped. Therefore, telemetry events for failures only work if you catch the error at a higher level or in a parent contract.
