Robust error handling is critical for production smart contracts. This guide demonstrates try-catch patterns, fallback logic, graceful degradation, transaction rollback, and comprehensive validation strategies in Soroban. Unaudited Example Code The example code in this pattern is for educational purposes and has not been audited for production use. Always conduct a thorough security audit before deploying to mainnet. Why Error Recovery Matters Smart contracts handle valuable assets and critical operations. Proper error handling prevents fund loss, ensures predictable behavior, and provides clear feedback when operations fail. Decision Tree Before choosing an error strategy, review the Error Handling concept decision tree for when to return Result, use panic!, or use panic_with_error!.
Rust stable and cargo Soroban CLI installed (setup guide) Understanding of Rust's Result type and error handling Familiarity with Soroban SDK error types

Soroban uses Rust's Result type for error handling, which is analogous to try-catch in other languages. Contract Test #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, contracttype, Env, Address, Symbol}; #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub enum Error { InsufficientBalance = 1, Unauthorized = 2, InvalidAmount = 3, TransferFailed = 4, } #[contract] pub struct TokenContract; #[contractimpl] impl TokenContract { /// Transfer with comprehensive error handling pub fn transfer( env: Env, from: Address, to: Address, amount: i128, ) -> Result<(), Error> { // Validate authorization from.require_auth(); // Validate inputs Self::validate_transfer(&env, &from, &to, amount)?; // Attempt transfer with error handling Self::execute_transfer(&env, &from, &to, amount)?; // Emit success event env.events().publish( (Symbol::new(&env, "transfer"), &from, &to), amount, ); Ok(()) } fn validate_transfer( env: &Env, from: &Address, to: &Address, amount: i128, ) -> Result<(), Error> { // Validate amount is positive if amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } // Validate addresses are different if from == to { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } // Check balance let balance = Self::get_balance(env, from); if balance < amount { return Err(Error::InsufficientBalance); } Ok(()) } fn execute_transfer( env: &Env, from: &Address, to: &Address, amount: i128, ) -> Result<(), Error> { let from_balance = Self::get_balance(env, from); let to_balance = Self::get_balance(env, to); // Perform atomic update env.storage().persistent().set(from, &(from_balance - amount)); env.storage().persistent().set(to, &(to_balance + amount)); Ok(()) } fn get_balance(env: &Env, addr: &Address) -> i128 { env.storage() .persistent() .get(addr) .unwrap_or(0) } } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; use soroban_sdk::{testutils::Address as _, Env}; #[test] fn test_successful_transfer() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register_contract(None, TokenContract); let client = TokenContractClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let alice = Address::generate(&env); let bob = Address::generate(&env); // Setup initial balance env.storage().persistent().set(&alice, &1000_i128); // Execute transfer env.mock_all_auths(); let result = client.try_transfer(&alice, &bob, &100); assert!(result.is_ok()); assert_eq!(client.get_balance(&alice), 900); assert_eq!(client.get_balance(&bob), 100); } #[test] fn test_insufficient_balance_error() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register_contract(None, TokenContract); let client = TokenContractClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let alice = Address::generate(&env); let bob = Address::generate(&env); env.storage().persistent().set(&alice, &50_i128); env.mock_all_auths(); let result = client.try_transfer(&alice, &bob, &100); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::InsufficientBalance))); } #[test] fn test_invalid_amount_error() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register_contract(None, TokenContract); let client = TokenContractClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let alice = Address::generate(&env); let bob = Address::generate(&env); env.mock_all_auths(); let result = client.try_transfer(&alice, &bob, &-100); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::InvalidAmount))); } } Best Practice Always use Result<T, Error> return types for functions that can fail. This makes error handling explicit and forces callers to handle potential failures.

Implement fallback mechanisms when primary operations fail. Contract Test #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, Env, Address, Symbol}; #[contract] pub struct PriceOracle; #[contractimpl] impl PriceOracle { /// Get price with fallback to secondary oracle pub fn get_price_with_fallback( env: Env, asset: Symbol, ) -> Result<i128, Error> { // Try primary oracle match Self::get_primary_price(&env, &asset) { Ok(price) => { env.events().publish( (Symbol::new(&env, "price_source"),), Symbol::new(&env, "primary"), ); Ok(price) } Err(_) => { // Fallback to secondary oracle match Self::get_secondary_price(&env, &asset) { Ok(price) => { env.events().publish( (Symbol::new(&env, "price_source"),), Symbol::new(&env, "secondary"), ); Ok(price) } Err(_) => { // Final fallback to cached price Self::get_cached_price(&env, &asset) .ok_or(Error::NoPriceAvailable) } } } } } fn get_primary_price(env: &Env, asset: &Symbol) -> Result<i128, Error> { env.storage() .persistent() .get(&(Symbol::new(env, "primary"), asset)) .ok_or(Error::PrimaryOracleFailed) } fn get_secondary_price(env: &Env, asset: &Symbol) -> Result<i128, Error> { env.storage() .persistent() .get(&(Symbol::new(env, "secondary"), asset)) .ok_or(Error::SecondaryOracleFailed) } fn get_cached_price(env: &Env, asset: &Symbol) -> Option<i128> { env.storage() .temporary() .get(&(Symbol::new(env, "cache"), asset)) } } #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub enum Error { PrimaryOracleFailed = 1, SecondaryOracleFailed = 2, NoPriceAvailable = 3, } #[test] fn test_fallback_to_secondary() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register_contract(None, PriceOracle); let client = PriceOracleClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let asset = Symbol::new(&env, "XLM"); // Primary fails, secondary succeeds env.storage().persistent().set( &(Symbol::new(&env, "secondary"), &asset), &100_i128, ); let price = client.get_price_with_fallback(&asset); assert_eq!(price, Ok(100)); } #[test] fn test_fallback_to_cache() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register_contract(None, PriceOracle); let client = PriceOracleClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let asset = Symbol::new(&env, "XLM"); // Both oracles fail, use cache env.storage().temporary().set( &(Symbol::new(&env, "cache"), &asset), &95_i128, ); let price = client.get_price_with_fallback(&asset); assert_eq!(price, Ok(95)); } Fallback Considerations Ensure fallback data sources are reliable and up-to-date. Stale cached data can lead to incorrect contract behavior.

Design contracts to continue operating with reduced functionality when errors occur. Contract Test #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, Env, Address, Symbol}; #[contract] pub struct DexContract; #[contractimpl] impl DexContract { /// Swap with graceful degradation pub fn swap_with_degradation( env: Env, user: Address, amount_in: i128, min_amount_out: i128, ) -> Result<SwapResult, Error> { user.require_auth(); // Try optimal routing match Self::try_optimal_swap(&env, &user, amount_in, min_amount_out) { Ok(result) => Ok(result), Err(Error::OptimalRouteFailed) => { // Degrade to direct swap env.events().publish( (Symbol::new(&env, "degraded_mode"),), Symbol::new(&env, "direct_swap"), ); Self::try_direct_swap(&env, &user, amount_in, min_amount_out) } Err(e) => Err(e), } } fn try_optimal_swap( env: &Env, user: &Address, amount_in: i128, min_amount_out: i128, ) -> Result<SwapResult, Error> { // Complex multi-hop routing let route = Self::calculate_optimal_route(env, amount_in)?; Self::execute_multi_hop_swap(env, user, &route, min_amount_out) } fn try_direct_swap( env: &Env, user: &Address, amount_in: i128, min_amount_out: i128, ) -> Result<SwapResult, Error> { // Simple direct pool swap let amount_out = Self::calculate_direct_swap(env, amount_in)?; if amount_out < min_amount_out { return Err(Error::SlippageTooHigh); } Self::execute_direct_swap(env, user, amount_in, amount_out) } fn calculate_optimal_route( env: &Env, amount_in: i128, ) -> Result<Vec<Address>, Error> { // Simulate route calculation that might fail env.storage() .temporary() .get(&Symbol::new(env, "route")) .ok_or(Error::OptimalRouteFailed) } fn execute_multi_hop_swap( env: &Env, user: &Address, route: &Vec<Address>, min_amount_out: i128, ) -> Result<SwapResult, Error> { // Execute complex swap Ok(SwapResult { amount_out: 1000, route_type: Symbol::new(env, "optimal"), }) } fn calculate_direct_swap(env: &Env, amount_in: i128) -> Result<i128, Error> { // Simple calculation Ok(amount_in * 95 / 100) // 5% slippage } fn execute_direct_swap( env: &Env, user: &Address, amount_in: i128, amount_out: i128, ) -> Result<SwapResult, Error> { Ok(SwapResult { amount_out, route_type: Symbol::new(env, "direct"), }) } } #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub struct SwapResult { pub amount_out: i128, pub route_type: Symbol, } #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub enum Error { OptimalRouteFailed = 1, SlippageTooHigh = 2, InsufficientLiquidity = 3, } #[test] fn test_graceful_degradation() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register_contract(None, DexContract); let client = DexContractClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let user = Address::generate(&env); // Optimal route not available, should degrade to direct env.mock_all_auths(); let result = client.swap_with_degradation(&user, &1000, &900); assert!(result.is_ok()); let swap_result = result.unwrap(); assert_eq!(swap_result.route_type, Symbol::new(&env, "direct")); } Graceful Degradation Benefits Graceful degradation ensures your contract remains functional even when optimal paths fail, improving reliability and user experience.

Soroban automatically rolls back state changes when a contract panics or returns an error. Contract Test #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, Env, Address}; #[contract] pub struct AtomicSwap; #[contractimpl] impl AtomicSwap { /// Atomic swap - all or nothing pub fn atomic_swap( env: Env, user_a: Address, user_b: Address, amount_a: i128, amount_b: i128, ) -> Result<(), Error> { user_a.require_auth(); user_b.require_auth(); // All operations succeed or all fail (automatic rollback) Self::validate_balances(&env, &user_a, &user_b, amount_a, amount_b)?; Self::execute_swap(&env, &user_a, &user_b, amount_a, amount_b)?; Self::emit_swap_event(&env, &user_a, &user_b, amount_a, amount_b); Ok(()) } fn validate_balances( env: &Env, user_a: &Address, user_b: &Address, amount_a: i128, amount_b: i128, ) -> Result<(), Error> { let balance_a = Self::get_balance(env, user_a); let balance_b = Self::get_balance(env, user_b); if balance_a < amount_a { // This error causes automatic rollback return Err(Error::InsufficientBalanceA); } if balance_b < amount_b { // This error causes automatic rollback return Err(Error::InsufficientBalanceB); } Ok(()) } fn execute_swap( env: &Env, user_a: &Address, user_b: &Address, amount_a: i128, amount_b: i128, ) -> Result<(), Error> { // These changes are atomic - all succeed or all rollback let balance_a = Self::get_balance(env, user_a); let balance_b = Self::get_balance(env, user_b); env.storage().persistent().set(user_a, &(balance_a - amount_a + amount_b)); env.storage().persistent().set(user_b, &(balance_b - amount_b + amount_a)); Ok(()) } fn emit_swap_event( env: &Env, user_a: &Address, user_b: &Address, amount_a: i128, amount_b: i128, ) { env.events().publish( (Symbol::new(env, "swap"), user_a, user_b), (amount_a, amount_b), ); } fn get_balance(env: &Env, addr: &Address) -> i128 { env.storage().persistent().get(addr).unwrap_or(0) } } #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub enum Error { InsufficientBalanceA = 1, InsufficientBalanceB = 2, } #[test] fn test_rollback_on_error() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register_contract(None, AtomicSwap); let client = AtomicSwapClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let alice = Address::generate(&env); let bob = Address::generate(&env); // Setup: Alice has 100, Bob has 50 env.storage().persistent().set(&alice, &100_i128); env.storage().persistent().set(&bob, &50_i128); env.mock_all_auths(); // Try to swap more than Bob has - should fail and rollback let result = client.try_atomic_swap(&alice, &bob, &50, &100); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::InsufficientBalanceB))); // Verify balances unchanged (rollback worked) assert_eq!(client.get_balance(&alice), 100); assert_eq!(client.get_balance(&bob), 50); } #[test] fn test_successful_atomic_swap() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register_contract(None, AtomicSwap); let client = AtomicSwapClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let alice = Address::generate(&env); let bob = Address::generate(&env); env.storage().persistent().set(&alice, &100_i128); env.storage().persistent().set(&bob, &200_i128); env.mock_all_auths(); let result = client.try_atomic_swap(&alice, &bob, &50, &100); assert!(result.is_ok()); assert_eq!(client.get_balance(&alice), 150); // 100 - 50 + 100 assert_eq!(client.get_balance(&bob), 150); // 200 - 100 + 50 } Automatic Rollback Soroban automatically rolls back all state changes when a contract returns an error or panics. You don't need to manually undo changes.

Validate all inputs early to fail fast and provide clear error messages. Contract Test #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, Env, Address, String}; #[contract] pub struct ValidatedContract; #[contractimpl] impl ValidatedContract { pub fn create_order( env: Env, user: Address, amount: i128, price: i128, expiry: u64, ) -> Result<u64, Error> { user.require_auth(); // Comprehensive validation Self::validate_order_params(&env, amount, price, expiry)?; // Execute business logic let order_id = Self::store_order(&env, &user, amount, price, expiry); Ok(order_id) } fn validate_order_params( env: &Env, amount: i128, price: i128, expiry: u64, ) -> Result<(), Error> { // Validate amount if amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } if amount > 1_000_000_000 { return Err(Error::AmountTooLarge); } // Validate price if price <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidPrice); } // Validate expiry let current_time = env.ledger().timestamp(); if expiry <= current_time { return Err(Error::ExpiryInPast); } let max_expiry = current_time + (30 * 24 * 60 * 60); // 30 days if expiry > max_expiry { return Err(Error::ExpiryTooFar); } Ok(()) } fn store_order( env: &Env, user: &Address, amount: i128, price: i128, expiry: u64, ) -> u64 { let order_id = Self::get_next_order_id(env); env.storage().persistent().set( &order_id, &Order { user: user.clone(), amount, price, expiry, }, ); order_id } fn get_next_order_id(env: &Env) -> u64 { let current: u64 = env.storage() .instance() .get(&Symbol::new(env, "order_id")) .unwrap_or(0); let next = current + 1; env.storage().instance().set(&Symbol::new(env, "order_id"), &next); next } } #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub struct Order { pub user: Address, pub amount: i128, pub price: i128, pub expiry: u64, } #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub enum Error { InvalidAmount = 1, AmountTooLarge = 2, InvalidPrice = 3, ExpiryInPast = 4, ExpiryTooFar = 5, } #[test] fn test_validation_invalid_amount() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register_contract(None, ValidatedContract); let client = ValidatedContractClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let user = Address::generate(&env); let expiry = env.ledger().timestamp() + 3600; env.mock_all_auths(); // Test negative amount let result = client.try_create_order(&user, &-100, &1000, &expiry); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::InvalidAmount))); // Test zero amount let result = client.try_create_order(&user, &0, &1000, &expiry); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::InvalidAmount))); // Test amount too large let result = client.try_create_order(&user, &2_000_000_000, &1000, &expiry); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::AmountTooLarge))); } #[test] fn test_validation_expiry() { let env = Env::default(); let contract_id = env.register_contract(None, ValidatedContract); let client = ValidatedContractClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let user = Address::generate(&env); let current_time = env.ledger().timestamp(); env.mock_all_auths(); // Test expiry in past let result = client.try_create_order(&user, &100, &1000, &(current_time - 1)); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::ExpiryInPast))); // Test expiry too far let far_future = current_time + (60 * 24 * 60 * 60); // 60 days let result = client.try_create_order(&user, &100, &1000, &far_future); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::ExpiryTooFar))); } Validation Best Practices Validate all inputs at function entry - Provide specific error types for different validation failures - Check business logic constraints (ranges, relationships) - Validate time-based parameters against ledger time

Critical Security Practices Never ignore errors: Always handle Result types explicitly Validate before state changes: Check all conditions before modifying storage Use specific error types: Avoid generic errors that hide root causes Test error paths: Write tests for every error condition Avoid panics in production: Use Result instead of panic! or unwrap()

// ❌ BAD: Ignoring errors let balance = env.storage().get(&user).unwrap(); // Can panic! // ✅ GOOD: Handling errors let balance = env.storage() .get(&user) .unwrap_or(0); // Safe default // ❌ BAD: Generic errors return Err(Error::Failed); // ✅ GOOD: Specific errors return Err(Error::InsufficientBalance); // ❌ BAD: State change before validation env.storage().set(&user, &new_balance); if new_balance < 0 { return Err(Error::Invalid); // Too late! } // ✅ GOOD: Validation before state change if new_balance < 0 { return Err(Error::Invalid); } env.storage().set(&user, &new_balance);

Before deploying your contract, verify: All functions that can fail return Result<T, Error> Custom error enum with specific error types Input validation at function entry No unwrap() or expect() calls in production code Fallback logic for external dependencies Comprehensive error tests Clear error messages in documentation Events emitted for important errors Graceful degradation where appropriate Atomic operations for multi-step processes

An educational two-party escrow contract with an arbiter for dispute resolution.

The escrow pattern is one of the most fundamental DeFi primitives. A buyer locks tokens inside the contract; a seller can only receive those tokens once the buyer (or arbiter) releases them. If a dispute arises, the arbiter can either release to the seller or refund the buyer. [Created] ──deposit──▶ [Funded] [Funded] ──release──▶ [Released] ← buyer or arbiter [Funded] ──refund───▶ [Refunded] ← arbiter only
Role Can Cannot Buyer Deposit funds, release to seller Refund themselves Seller Receive released funds Trigger any state change Arbiter Release to seller, refund buyer Nothing else

Unaudited Educational Example — Not for Production This contract pattern is an educational example and has not undergone an independent security audit. Do not deploy this snippet to production or mainnet with real funds without substantial hardening, complete test coverage, and formal verification. Security & Architectural Limitations: Authentication & Authorization: Every state-modifying action requires explicit caller verification (buyer.require_auth() in deposit(), caller.require_auth() checked against buyer or arbiter in release(), and caller.require_auth() restricted strictly to arbiter in refund()). Note that initialize() in this educational snippet does not enforce caller authorization, allowing anyone to initialize an uninitialized contract instance. Reentrancy: State updates (EscrowState::Funded, Released, Refunded) should be written following checks-effects-interactions principles before external token contract calls. In Soroban's synchronous cross-contract execution model, token transfers resolve atomically; however, if external untrusted callbacks or token contracts are involved, effects must be finalized prior to external interactions. Storage TTL & Data Expiry: All contract entries (Buyer, Seller, Arbiter, Token, Amount, State) are stored in persistent storage. While persistent storage entries survive contract archiving and can be restored, they possess a finite time-to-live (TTL) on the ledger. Production deployments must routinely monitor and extend entry TTLs using env.storage().persistent().extend_ttl(...) to prevent escrow data from becoming archived and temporarily unusable. escrow_basic/src/lib.rs Cargo.toml #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contracterror, contractimpl, contracttype, token, Address, Env}; #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone)] pub enum DataKey { Buyer, Seller, Arbiter, Token, Amount, State, } #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub enum EscrowState { Created, Funded, Released, Refunded, } #[contracterror] #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq, PartialOrd, Ord)] #[repr(u32)] pub enum Error { AlreadyInitialized = 1, NotInitialized = 2, InvalidAmount = 3, NotFunded = 4, UnauthorizedRelease = 5, UnauthorizedRefund = 6, AlreadySettled = 7, } #[contract] pub struct EscrowBasic; #[contractimpl] impl EscrowBasic { /// Set up the escrow — no funds move yet. pub fn initialize( env: Env, buyer: Address, seller: Address, arbiter: Address, token: Address, amount: i128, ) -> Result<(), Error> { if env.storage().persistent().has(&DataKey::State) { return Err(Error::AlreadyInitialized); } if amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Buyer, &buyer); env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Seller, &seller); env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Arbiter, &arbiter); env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Token, &token); env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Amount, &amount); env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::State, &EscrowState::Created); Ok(()) } /// Buyer deposits funds. Moves state to Funded. pub fn deposit(env: Env) -> Result<(), Error> { let state: EscrowState = env.storage().persistent() .get(&DataKey::State).ok_or(Error::NotInitialized)?; if state != EscrowState::Created { return Err(Error::AlreadySettled); } let buyer: Address = env.storage().persistent() .get(&DataKey::Buyer).ok_or(Error::NotInitialized)?; buyer.require_auth(); let token: Address = env.storage().persistent() .get(&DataKey::Token).ok_or(Error::NotInitialized)?; let amount: i128 = env.storage().persistent() .get(&DataKey::Amount).ok_or(Error::NotInitialized)?; token::Client::new(&env, &token) .transfer(&buyer, &env.current_contract_address(), &amount); env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::State, &EscrowState::Funded); Ok(()) } /// Release funds to seller. Caller must be buyer or arbiter. pub fn release(env: Env, caller: Address) -> Result<(), Error> { caller.require_auth(); let state: EscrowState = env.storage().persistent() .get(&DataKey::State).ok_or(Error::NotInitialized)?; if state != EscrowState::Funded { return Err(Error::NotFunded); } let buyer: Address = env.storage().persistent() .get(&DataKey::Buyer).ok_or(Error::NotInitialized)?; let arbiter: Address = env.storage().persistent() .get(&DataKey::Arbiter).ok_or(Error::NotInitialized)?; if caller != buyer && caller != arbiter { return Err(Error::UnauthorizedRelease); } let seller: Address = env.storage().persistent() .get(&DataKey::Seller).ok_or(Error::NotInitialized)?; let token: Address = env.storage().persistent() .get(&DataKey::Token).ok_or(Error::NotInitialized)?; let amount: i128 = env.storage().persistent() .get(&DataKey::Amount).ok_or(Error::NotInitialized)?; token::Client::new(&env, &token) .transfer(&env.current_contract_address(), &seller, &amount); env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::State, &EscrowState::Released); Ok(()) } /// Refund buyer. Caller must be arbiter. pub fn refund(env: Env, caller: Address) -> Result<(), Error> { caller.require_auth(); let state: EscrowState = env.storage().persistent() .get(&DataKey::State).ok_or(Error::NotInitialized)?; if state != EscrowState::Funded { return Err(Error::NotFunded); } let arbiter: Address = env.storage().persistent() .get(&DataKey::Arbiter).ok_or(Error::NotInitialized)?; if caller != arbiter { return Err(Error::UnauthorizedRefund); } let buyer: Address = env.storage().persistent() .get(&DataKey::Buyer).ok_or(Error::NotInitialized)?; let token: Address = env.storage().persistent() .get(&DataKey::Token).ok_or(Error::NotInitialized)?; let amount: i128 = env.storage().persistent() .get(&DataKey::Amount).ok_or(Error::NotInitialized)?; token::Client::new(&env, &token) .transfer(&env.current_contract_address(), &buyer, &amount); env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::State, &EscrowState::Refunded); Ok(()) } pub fn get_state(env: Env) -> Option<EscrowState> { env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::State) } pub fn get_amount(env: Env) -> Option<i128> { env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::Amount) } } [package] name = "escrow-basic" version = "0.1.0" edition = "2021" [lib] crate-type = ["cdylib", "rlib"] [dependencies] soroban-sdk = { version = "22.0.0", features = ["testutils"] } [dev-dependencies] soroban-sdk = { version = "22.0.0", features = ["testutils"] } [profile.release] opt-level = "z" overflow-checks = true debug = 0 strip = "symbols" debug-assertions = false panic = "abort" codegen-units = 1 lto = true
All parameters (buyer, seller, arbiter, token, amount) are stored during initialize. This keeps deposit simple and prevents parameters being swapped at deposit time.
documents.s: Why does deposit take no arguments?

documents.t: This is intentional. If the buyer could refund unilaterally they could abuse the escrow as a free option — deposit, wait, and refund if the deal is no longer favourable. The arbiter acts as the tiebreaker.
documents.s: Why can't the buyer refund themselves?

documents.t: All state uses persistent storage (not instance or temporary). This means entries survive TTL expiry when extended, which is important for escrows that may sit idle for weeks.

Reentrancy: Soroban's execution model prevents reentrancy — each contract invocation is atomic and cross-contract calls resolve synchronously. Integer overflow: overflow-checks = true in the release profile catches arithmetic overflows at runtime. Access control: Every state-changing function validates the caller against stored role addresses. require_auth() enforces on-chain authorisation.

A production-ready escrow contract with three roles — depositor, recipient, and arbitrator — and a built-in dispute resolution path. Info Difficulty: Intermediate | Category: Utility | Source: examples/escrow-multiparty

Standard two-party escrows break down when buyer and seller disagree. This contract adds a neutral arbitrator who can step in when either party raises a dispute, making it suitable for real-world trade, freelance payments, and marketplace transactions.

PENDING ──release()──► RELEASED ──cancel()───► CANCELLED (depositor only) ──dispute()──► DISPUTED │ resolve()├──► RELEASED (arbitrator rules for recipient) └──► CANCELLED (arbitrator rules for depositor)
Role Can do Depositor Fund escrow, release to recipient, cancel (Pending only), open dispute Recipient Open dispute Arbitrator Resolve a disputed escrow in either direction

Unaudited Educational Example — Not for Production This contract pattern is an educational example and has not undergone an independent security audit. Do not deploy this snippet to production or mainnet without substantial hardening, complete test coverage, and formal review. Security & Architectural Limitations: Reentrancy: The contract uses a checks-effects pattern, updating state flags in instance storage before returning amounts. Because it operates on an abstract numerical amount (i128) without performing external token transfers or callee callbacks, external reentrancy vectors do not directly apply. If extended to invoke external token contracts (such as Stellar Asset Contracts or custom tokens), token transfers must occur strictly after all state modifications, or a reentrancy guard should be utilized. Storage TTL & Data Expiry: All escrow state and party addresses are saved in instance storage. In Soroban, instance storage entries share the contract instance's time-to-live (TTL). If the instance TTL is not monitored and extended via env.storage().instance().extend_ttl(...) before expiration, the escrow data will become archived/inaccessible, locking state transitions until restored. #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contracterror, contractimpl, contracttype, Address, Env}; #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, Eq, PartialEq)] pub enum State { Pending, Disputed, Released, Cancelled, } #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone)] pub enum DataKey { Depositor, Recipient, Arbitrator, Amount, State, } #[contracterror] #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq, PartialOrd, Ord)] #[repr(u32)] pub enum Error { AlreadyInitialised = 1, NotInitialised = 2, InvalidAmount = 3, Unauthorised = 4, InvalidState = 5, } #[contract] pub struct EscrowMultiparty; #[contractimpl] impl EscrowMultiparty { /// Lock funds into the escrow. pub fn deposit( env: Env, depositor: Address, recipient: Address, arbitrator: Address, amount: i128, ) -> Result<(), Error> { depositor.require_auth(); if env.storage().instance().has(&DataKey::State) { return Err(Error::AlreadyInitialised); } if amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::Depositor, &depositor); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::Recipient, &recipient); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::Arbitrator, &arbitrator); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::Amount, &amount); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::State, &State::Pending); Ok(()) } /// Depositor releases funds to the recipient (Pending only). pub fn release(env: Env) -> Result<i128, Error> { let depositor: Address = env.storage().instance() .get(&DataKey::Depositor).ok_or(Error::NotInitialised)?; depositor.require_auth(); Self::require_state(&env, State::Pending)?; let amount = Self::get_amount_inner(&env)?; env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::State, &State::Released); Ok(amount) } /// Depositor cancels and reclaims funds (Pending only). pub fn cancel(env: Env) -> Result<i128, Error> { let depositor: Address = env.storage().instance() .get(&DataKey::Depositor).ok_or(Error::NotInitialised)?; depositor.require_auth(); Self::require_state(&env, State::Pending)?; let amount = Self::get_amount_inner(&env)?; env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::State, &State::Cancelled); Ok(amount) } /// Depositor or recipient raises a dispute (Pending only). pub fn dispute(env: Env, caller: Address) -> Result<(), Error> { caller.require_auth(); let depositor: Address = env.storage().instance() .get(&DataKey::Depositor).ok_or(Error::NotInitialised)?; let recipient: Address = env.storage().instance() .get(&DataKey::Recipient).ok_or(Error::NotInitialised)?; if caller != depositor && caller != recipient { return Err(Error::Unauthorised); } Self::require_state(&env, State::Pending)?; env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::State, &State::Disputed); Ok(()) } /// Arbitrator resolves a dispute (Disputed only). /// /// Pass `true` to release funds to the recipient, `false` to refund the depositor. pub fn resolve(env: Env, release_to_recipient: bool) -> Result<i128, Error> { let arbitrator: Address = env.storage().instance() .get(&DataKey::Arbitrator).ok_or(Error::NotInitialised)?; arbitrator.require_auth(); Self::require_state(&env, State::Disputed)?; let amount = Self::get_amount_inner(&env)?; let new_state = if release_to_recipient { State::Released } else { State::Cancelled }; env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::State, &new_state); Ok(amount) } // ── View helpers ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── pub fn state(env: Env) -> Result<State, Error> { env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::State).ok_or(Error::NotInitialised) } pub fn get_amount(env: Env) -> Result<i128, Error> { Self::get_amount_inner(&env) } pub fn get_depositor(env: Env) -> Result<Address, Error> { env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::Depositor).ok_or(Error::NotInitialised) } pub fn get_recipient(env: Env) -> Result<Address, Error> { env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::Recipient).ok_or(Error::NotInitialised) } pub fn get_arbitrator(env: Env) -> Result<Address, Error> { env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::Arbitrator).ok_or(Error::NotInitialised) } // ── Internal ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── fn get_amount_inner(env: &Env) -> Result<i128, Error> { env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::Amount).ok_or(Error::NotInitialised) } fn require_state(env: &Env, expected: State) -> Result<(), Error> { let current: State = env.storage().instance() .get(&DataKey::State).ok_or(Error::NotInitialised)?; if current != expected { return Err(Error::InvalidState); } Ok(()) } }

Two-party escrows give the depositor (buyer) the power to cancel at any time, which puts the recipient (seller/freelancer) at risk. Adding a neutral arbitrator removes that imbalance: once a dispute is raised, only the arbitrator decides the outcome.

Every state-changing call verifies the caller's identity first: depositor.require_auth(); // verify before reading/writing state This follows Soroban's authorization model — auth checks must happen before any effects so the runtime can correctly attribute them.

State is written before returning the amount, ensuring no re-entrancy through cross-contract calls: env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::State, &State::Released); // effect first Ok(amount) // then return value

All functions guard their entry condition with a single helper instead of duplicating the check: fn require_state(env: &Env, expected: State) -> Result<(), Error> { let current: State = env.storage().instance() .get(&DataKey::State).ok_or(Error::NotInitialised)?; if current != expected { return Err(Error::InvalidState); } Ok(()) }

The crate's test module covers every state transition. The dispute resolution tests are: #[test] fn test_resolve_in_favour_of_recipient() { let (_, actors, client) = funded(1_000); client.dispute(&actors.recipient).unwrap(); // recipient opens dispute assert_eq!(client.resolve(&true), Ok(1_000)); // arbitrator rules for recipient assert_eq!(client.state(), Ok(State::Released)); } #[test] fn test_resolve_in_favour_of_depositor() { let (_, actors, client) = funded(1_000); client.dispute(&actors.depositor).unwrap(); // depositor opens dispute assert_eq!(client.resolve(&false), Ok(1_000)); // arbitrator refunds depositor assert_eq!(client.state(), Ok(State::Cancelled)); } Run the tests: cd examples/escrow-multiparty cargo test

Expiry time — auto-cancel if the recipient never disputes after a deadline (combine with the Timelock Vault pattern). Partial release — split the amount between parties when the arbitrator decides neither side is fully at fault. Token integration — replace the i128 amount with a real token transfer using the Token Interface. Multi-sig arbitration — require M-of-N arbitrators to agree before resolving, removing single-point-of-failure trust in one arbitrator.

A flash loan is a single-asset liquidity pool that lets anyone borrow tokens with no collateral, provided the loan (plus a fee) is repaid before the borrowing transaction finishes. This pattern demonstrates how to implement a Flash Loan pool in Soroban. Because the Soroban host aborts the whole invocation and rolls back state changes if the transaction panics, an unpaid loan simply never takes effect. Prerequisites Rust and soroban-sdk version 22+ Familiarity with cross-contract calls (contractclient) Understanding of transaction rollbacks on panic Implementation Unaudited Educational Example — Not for Production This contract pattern is an educational example and has not undergone an independent security audit. Do not deploy this snippet to production or mainnet without substantial hardening, complete test coverage, and formal review. Security & Architectural Limitations: Authorization & require_auth: The pool's public flash_loan entrypoint intentionally does not require caller authentication because flash loans are permissionless by design. However, administrative functions (such as initialize and withdraw_fees) require explicit admin.require_auth() authorization, and deposit_liquidity requires from.require_auth(). Furthermore, the receiver's execute_operation callback must verify that the calling pool matches the expected pool address to prevent unauthorized execution or spoofed callback attacks. Storage TTL & Data Expiry: The pool's configuration (Admin, Token, FeeBps, FeesCollected) is stored in instance storage. In Soroban, instance storage entries share the contract instance's time-to-live (TTL). If the instance TTL is not routinely monitored and extended via env.storage().instance().extend_ttl(...), the contract and its state will expire, disabling flash loan operations until restored. The Receiver Interface​ The contract receiving the flash loan must implement a specific interface. The pool transfers the borrowed tokens to the receiver and then calls execute_operation. #[contractclient(name = "FlashLoanReceiverClient")] pub trait FlashLoanReceiverInterface { fn execute_operation(env: Env, pool: Address, asset: Address, amount: i128, fee: i128); } Atomic Repayment and Fee​ The pool implements the flash_loan function. It calculates the fee, transfers the tokens to the receiver, invokes the receiver's callback, and then verifies that the pool's balance has increased by at least the required fee. pub fn flash_loan(env: Env, receiver: Address, amount: i128) -> Result<i128, Error> { // ... validation and setup ... let fee = Self::calculate_fee(env.clone(), amount); // Interaction: hand the principal to the receiver before we know // whether it will be repaid. token_client.transfer(&pool, &receiver, &amount); // Arbitrary receiver logic runs here (e.g. arbitrage). FlashLoanReceiverClient::new(&env, &receiver).execute_operation( &pool, &token_addr, &amount, &fee, ); // Effects: verify repayment by re-reading the pool's own balance let balance_after = token_client.balance(&pool); let required = balance_before.checked_add(fee).expect("overflow"); if balance_after < required { panic!("flash-loan: repayment not received"); } // ... update fees collected ... Ok(fee) } Testing the Non-Repay Scenario The examples/flash-loan contract includes a test specifically verifying that if the receiver does not repay the loan, the transaction reverts and the state is unchanged. #[test] fn test_failed_flash_loan_leaves_pool_state_untouched() { let (env, _admin, _lp, token_addr, client) = setup(); let borrower_id = env.register(NoRepayBorrower, ()); let result = std::panic::catch_unwind(std::panic::AssertUnwindSafe(|| { client.flash_loan(&borrower_id, &500); })); assert!(result.is_err(), "flash loan should have panicked"); // The host rolls back the whole invocation on panic, so the // principal transfer to the borrower never actually happened. let token_client = token::Client::new(&env, &token_addr); assert_eq!(token_client.balance(&client.address), 1_000); assert_eq!(token_client.balance(&borrower_id), 0); } This explains the non-repay test scenario and proves the atomic nature of the flash loan, which is correctly enforced by the Soroban environment. Security & Reentrancy Because the balance check happens after control returns from the receiver, the contract never trusts the receiver's return value for the critical invariant — it verifies the token balance directly. This mirrors the checks-effects-interactions discipline used in the Reentrancy Guard pattern, applied to a borrow-repay invariant instead of a double-spend invariant. The transaction's atomic rollback capability eliminates the need for complex internal mutex lock state flags for the repayment mechanic itself. See the DeFi Security Guide for more details. title: HTLC Atomic Swap assets: swap script hashlock timelock

An atomic swap using Hash Time Lock Contracts (HTLC) enables two parties to exchange assets without trust. This pattern is useful for atomic cross-chain swaps, payment channels, and other decentralized financial interactions.

The HTLC pattern relies on three primitives: HASH LOCK: The payee claims funds by providing the preimage of a given hash. TIME LOCK: Unclaimed funds are returned to the payer after a deadline. REFUND: The sender can recover funds if the receiver fails to claim them in time. For details on Bytes, fixed-size BytesN, hash outputs, and common conversion mistakes, see Bytes, BytesN, and Hashes.

The Hash Time Lock Contract creates a funding box that locks funds until it either receives the preimage of a given hash or after a specified deadline passes. Here is the step-by-step process: A secret preimage is generated by one party (i.e., A). Its hash is shared. A creates an HTLC script on chain X, funding it with asset A and a timelock. B creates an HTLC script on chain Y, funding it with asset B and a shorter timelock. B claims the funds on chain X by revealing the preimage. A uses that preimage to claim the funds on chain Y. If B draws out, A refunds from chain V after timeout.

This pattern carries two important security musts: High Confidentiality: The preimage must be known only to the sender and the receiver, as revealing it to a third party could allow them to claim funds. Clock Synchronization: The timelocks must be set correctly to avoid one party forfeiting funds unfairly. Whatever activity is more critical should have a long enough buffer. Learner Safety & Production Warning The example contract material below is unaudited and provided strictly for educational purposes. Do not use this material in production without independent audits and full implementation of authentication, timelocks, and state handling.

Implementation Note: The code snippets below present the conceptual interface for HTLC functions. Production implementations require explicit authorization (require_auth), strict timelock validations against ledger sequence/timestamp, re-entrancy prevention, and storage TTL management. Authorization Expectations: Callers initiating swaps or claiming/refunding funds must authenticate via require_auth() (e.g. sender.require_auth() / receiver.require_auth()) to prevent unauthorized claims or premature refunds. Re-entrancy Limits: Token transfers triggered during claim or refund operations must execute after state mutations (checks-effects-interactions pattern) or be protected by re-entrancy guards to prevent reentrant claim/refund exploits. Storage TTL & Data Expiry: HTLC entries stored in contract storage (instance or temporary/persistent) are subject to Soroban ledger storage TTL limits. If an HTLC entry expires before the timelock refund period elapses, the entry must be restored via TTL extension before refund() can be executed. The following code snippets are taken from examples/htlc-swap/src/lib.rs. Hash Lock Time Lock Refund /// Creates an HTLC script with a hashlock and timeout. pub fn create_htlc(wit: Amount, hash: [u8; 32], timelock: BlockCount) /// Expires the HTLC script, in case the preimage is never revealed. pub fn refund(with: Amount) /// Returns funds to the sender once the time lock expires. pub fn refund(with: Amount)
The crate includes unit tests that cover the normal swap path and the refund path. Run them with the following command: cargo test--package htlc-swap

When deploying an Application using the Her lock Pattern: Ensure the contracts are deployed on the Appropriate networks. Set the deadline according to the block time and imaged response delay. Monitor chain confirmation times to avoid a one-block reordering attack.

In the world of immutable ledgers, contract upgrades are among the most sensitive operations a developer can perform. A Mistake in an upgrade can result in permanent loss of state, locked funds, or protocol insolvency. This guide treats contract upgrades as high-risk, irreversible operations requiring rigorous governance and verification. Safety First Always simulate upgrades and migrations on a local sandbox or testnet before executing on mainnet. Once state is corrupted on-chain, recovery is often impossible. Unaudited example — not for production This page is intentionally educational. The example contracts and copy-paste snippets are not audited, not designed for production governance, and should not be deployed with real funds or user assets. The upgrade pattern shown here is a teaching reference for how env.deployer().update_current_contract_wasm() and storage migration work in Soroban. It does not replace a production security review, emergency-response plan, or operational controls for rollback, monitoring, and governance. Reentrancy is not the main risk in the minimal upgrade flow shown on this page because the contract does not call an external contract during the upgrade itself. The upgrade function only authorizes the admin and calls update_current_contract_wasm(). Still, any custom migration or post-upgrade hook that makes external calls must be treated as reentrancy-sensitive and secured with the same care as other cross-contract entry points. Storage TTL is finite. Soroban persistent and instance entries age out unless their TTL is extended; temporary entries are deleted. Network minimums are roughly min_persistent_entry_ttl ≈ 4,096 ledgers and min_temp_entry_ttl ≈ 16 ledgers, with a practical maximum extension cap around max_entry_ttl ≈ 6,312,000 ledgers. If a protocol stores version markers, ownership data, or balances in persistent storage, you must explicitly manage TTL and archival/restoration behavior or the state can expire or be restored at a higher cost.
A (healthy protocol moves through distinct phases, each with specific entry and exit criteria.
Criteria: Code is feature-complete and passes all unit/integration tests. Action: Internal or external security audit of the Wasm bytecode and source logic. Exit: No high-severity issues remain.

Criteria: Deployment of the exact audited bytecode to a live network environment. Action: Manual QA, integration testing with front-end, and "chaos testing" (e.g., simulating high load). Exit: Contract behaves as expected in a multi-user environment.
Criteria: Final verification of initialization arguments and governance keys. Action: Atomic deployment and initialization. Exit: Success events emitted; state invariants verified.
Criteria: Ongoing operation. Action: Monitoring events, transaction volume, and potential anomalies. *Exit:** Identification of a bug or requirement for a feature upgrade.

Criteria: A newer version is ready or the feature is sunset. Action: "Sunset" phase where new deposits are disabled but withdrawals remain open. *Exit:** All funds removed; storage entries deleted where possible.

Upgrades must be protected by strict access control. In Soroban, the upgrade function should typically require the authorization of an admin or a decentralized governance body. Adding access control to the upgrade function Insecure (before)Authorized (after) 1#{contractimpl} 2impl MyContract { 3 pub fn upgrade(env: Env, new_wasm_hash: BytesN<32>) { 4 // Anyone can upgrade the contract — dangerous! 8 env.deployer().update_current_contract_wasm(new_wasm_hash); 9 } 11} 1#{contractimpl} 2impl MyContract { 3 pub fn upgrade(env: Env, new_wasm_hash: BytesN<32>) { 5 let admin: Address = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::Admin).unwrap(); 6 admin.require_auth(); // Ensure only the authorized admin can upgrade 7 8 env.deployer().update_current_contract_wasm(new_wasm_hash); 9 } 10 11} Governance Best Practice For high-value protocols, avoid single-key admin accounts. Use a multi-signature account or a DOA with a mandatory timelock (e.g., 7 days) to allow users to exit if they disagree with a pending upgrade.
Soroban provides native support for updating contract logic while preserving the contract ID and storage.

The most common way to upgrade is to call env.deployer().update_current_contract_wasm(). This replaces the contract's executable code with the bytecode associated with the provided Wasm hash. Use when: You need to fix a bug or add features without changing the contract's address. Avoid when: You need to change the fundamental architecture or storage model in a way that is incompatible with existing state. The canonical Soroban learning path in this repository is this guide, followed by the tested upgradeable example. It demonstrates an admin-gated self-upgrade, storage preservation, and lazy migration. It is the only Soroban upgrade implementation currently included; proxy, proxy-admin, beacon, and factory upgrade architectures are out of scope. The similarly named multisig-timelock-upgrade directory is a CosmWasm crate, not a Soroban example, and is not part of this learning path.

examples/upgradeable/src/lib.rs — contract with upgrade gated by admin.require_auth(). examples/upgradeable/v2 — the upgraded contract used in the upgrade tests; CI builds v2 first to produce the target Wasm. examples/upgradeable/src/test.rs — covers admin authorization, state preservation, migration, and double-migration protection. The upgrade test flow installs the v2 Wasm hash, invokes upgrade as the admin, then verifies the contract ID and storage are preserved while the code hash matches the v2 build.
When you upgrade logic, you often need to evolve the data structures in storage.

Upgrade individual storage entries only when they are accessed. This spreads the gas cost over many transactions and avoids hitting gas limits. ##{contracttype} pub enum AccountState { V3(AccountV1), V2(AccountV2), } pub fn get_account_v2(env: &Env, user: Address) -> AccountV2 { let state: AccountState = env.storage().persistent().get(&user).unwrap(); match state { AccountState::V1(v1) => { let upgraded = AccountV2 { balance: v1.balance, rewards: 0, // Initialize new field }; // Save the upgraded state back to storage env.storage().persistent().set(&user, &AccountState::V2(upgraded.clone())); upgraded } AccountState::V2(v2) => v2, } }

Perform the entire migration in a single transaction or a series of transactions. *Risk:** High gas consumption. May fail if the dataset is too large. *Best for:** Small, fixed-size datasets (e.g., global configuration).

[] Smoke tests pass (basic deposits/withdrawals). [] State invariants remain valid (e.g., Total Supply = sum of Balances). [] Version markers in storage have been updated. [] Events are being emitted correctly.

If an upgrade introduces a critical flaw, you must have a plan to recover. Immutable Fallback: If the contract is truly immutable, you cannot upgrade. Your only "rollback" is to deploy a new contract and ask users to migrate. Logic Rollback: Call upgrade again with the hash of the previous stable Wasm bytecode. Emergency Pause: Include a "Circuit Breaker" to halt operations while you diagnose and fix a failed upgrade. A multi-token vault keeps per-user, per-token accounting in a single contract. Any address may deposit any number of different tokens; the vault records each balance independently and allows partial or full withdrawals at any time.

Consolidated custody for DeFi protocols handling multiple assets Portfolio or yield-bearing vaults that accept arbitrary tokens Any contract that needs to track balances for several tokens without deploying one vault per asset Learning how compound storage keys work in Soroban

deposit(depositor, token, amount) └─ adds `amount` to Balance(depositor, token) and VaultTotal(token) withdraw(withdrawer, token, amount) └─ deducts `amount` from Balance(withdrawer, token) and VaultTotal(token) └─ reverts if balance is insufficient balance(user, token) └─ read-only: returns Balance(user, token), or 0 if never deposited vault_total(token) └─ read-only: returns the sum of all deposits for a token

Key Type Storage Description Balance(user, token) i128 instance Deposited balance per (user, token) VaultTotal(token) i128 instance Sum of all balances for a token The compound key Balance(user, token) is the core of the pattern — it encodes both the depositor address and the token address into a single storage entry without a nested map abstraction. Instance vs. persistent storage This example uses instance storage for simplicity. A production vault should use persistent storage and extend entry TTLs to ensure balances survive beyond the default ledger expiry window. Learner Safety & Production Warning The example contract code on this page is unaudited and provided strictly for educational purposes. Do not use this material in production without thorough security audits and comprehensive test suites. Safeguards & Architectural Limits Authorization: deposit and withdraw require explicit caller authorization via depositor.require_auth() and withdrawer.require_auth() to prevent unauthorized balance manipulations. Re-entrancy Limits: Uses the checks-effects pattern (updating internal balance state before external operations) to ensure re-entrancy safety. Note that Soroban's core host execution model also prevents direct cross-contract reentrancy by default. Storage TTL & Data Expiry: Currently uses instance storage for demonstration simplicity. Production vaults tracking long-term user assets should utilize persistent storage for user balances (env.storage().persistent()) and regularly extend entry TTLs (extend_ttl) to prevent balance data expiry.

examples/multi-token-vault/src/lib.rs #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contracterror, contractimpl, contracttype, Address, Env}; #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone)] pub enum DataKey { /// Per-user, per-token deposited balance. Balance(Address, Address), /// Vault-wide total deposits for a given token. VaultTotal(Address), } #[contracterror] #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq, PartialOrd, Ord)] #[repr(u32)] pub enum Error { /// Deposit or withdraw amount must be greater than zero. InvalidAmount = 1, /// Withdrawal exceeds the caller's recorded balance for that token. InsufficientBalance = 2, } #[contract] pub struct MultiTokenVault; #[contractimpl] impl MultiTokenVault { pub fn deposit(env: Env, depositor: Address, token: Address, amount: i128) -> Result<(), Error> { depositor.require_auth(); if amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } let balance_key = DataKey::Balance(depositor.clone(), token.clone()); let current: i128 = env.storage().instance().get(&balance_key).unwrap_or(0_i128); env.storage().instance().set(&balance_key, &(current + amount)); let total_key = DataKey::VaultTotal(token); let vault_total: i128 = env.storage().instance().get(&total_key).unwrap_or(0_i128); env.storage().instance().set(&total_key, &(vault_total + amount)); Ok(()) } pub fn withdraw( env: Env, withdrawer: Address, token: Address, amount: i128, ) -> Result<i128, Error> { withdrawer.require_auth(); if amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } let balance_key = DataKey::Balance(withdrawer.clone(), token.clone()); let current: i128 = env.storage().instance().get(&balance_key).unwrap_or(0_i128); if current < amount { return Err(Error::InsufficientBalance); } // Checks-effects: update state before any external interaction. env.storage().instance().set(&balance_key, &(current - amount)); let total_key = DataKey::VaultTotal(token); let vault_total: i128 = env.storage().instance().get(&total_key).unwrap_or(0_i128); env.storage().instance().set(&total_key, &(vault_total - amount)); Ok(amount) } pub fn balance(env: Env, user: Address, token: Address) -> i128 { env.storage() .instance() .get(&DataKey::Balance(user, token)) .unwrap_or(0_i128) } pub fn vault_total(env: Env, token: Address) -> i128 { env.storage() .instance() .get(&DataKey::VaultTotal(token)) .unwrap_or(0_i128) } }

The DataKey::Balance(Address, Address) variant stores both the user address and the token address inside the enum variant. Soroban serialises the whole variant — including the embedded addresses — into a single storage key. This replaces what would be a nested map in other environments with a flat key-value store entry, which is both simpler and more storage-efficient. // One entry per (user, token) pair — no nested maps needed. let key = DataKey::Balance(user.clone(), token.clone()); let balance: i128 = env.storage().instance().get(&key).unwrap_or(0);

A separate VaultTotal(token) key accumulates all deposits for a given token. This enables O(1) liquidity checks without iterating all user balances. let total: i128 = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::VaultTotal(token)).unwrap_or(0);

State is updated before returning the amount to the caller. This makes the intent explicit and matches best-practice even though Soroban's execution model already prevents reentrancy at the host level.

The contract records amounts in storage but does not call SAC (Stellar Asset Contract) transfer functions — it is intentionally scoped to teach the multi-asset accounting pattern without cross-contract complexity. See the token-transfer example for how to wire up actual token movement.

A multisig wallet requires a defined number of authorized signers to approve a transaction before it can be executed. This pattern demonstrates M-of-N authorization, where threshold signers must approve a proposal for it to become executable.

The multisig-wallet contract enables a group of users to manage shared funds or perform privileged operations collectively. It supports: Threshold management - set the number of approvals required Approval - signers approve a proposal Execution - execute a proposal once threshold is met Revocation - withdraw an approval before execution

Familiarity with Soroban authorization Understanding of contract storage Basic Rust and Soroban development setup Learner Safety & Production Warning The example contract code on this page is unaudited and provided strictly for educational purposes. Do not use this material in production without independent security audits and production-grade key management safeguards.

Storage TTL & Data Expiry Limits Storage Expiry: Proposals and signer configuration stored in contract storage are subject to Soroban ledger storage TTL limits. TTL Extension Requirement: In active multisig deployments, active proposal entries and contract instance storage must have their TTL extended (env.storage().persistent().extend_ttl(...) or instance().extend_ttl(...)) prior to expiration; expired proposal state will become inaccessible or require ledger restoration before approve or execute can proceed. The full implementation is available in examples/multisig-wallet/src/lib.rs. The contract stores a list of signers, the current threshold, and a map of proposals from their id to approval states.

Function Description set_threshold(new_threshold) Updates the approval threshold. Must be between 1 and the total number of signers. approve(proposal_id) Marks the caller as approving the given proposal. Callable only by authorized signers. execute(proposal_id) Executes the proposal if the number of approvals meets or exceeds the current threshold. revoke(proposal_id) Removes the caller's approval, potentially dropping the proposal below threshold.

1-of-1 wallet - With a single signer and threshold 1, the wallet behaves like a simple owner-controlled account. Approval and execution happen in one step. Threshold equals signer count - Requires unanimous approval (N-of-N). Threshold greater than signer count - Invalid; the contract should reject such values. Changing threshold after approvals - Existing approvals remain, but the new threshold applies to future executions.

The example's test suite covers these critical paths: Setting a valid threshold Rejecting an invalid threshold (e.g., 0 or greater than signer count) Approving with exactly enough signers to reach the threshold Executing only after the threshold has been satisfied Revoking an approval to drop below threshold, blocking execution Attempting to approve or execute without authorization

Authorization - Always verify env.current_contract_address( and require authentication for signers using require_auth. Error handling - Use panic, or a custom Error type for unauthorized calls, duplicate approvals, invalid thresholds, and proposals that don't exist. Event emission - Emit approval, execution, and revocation events to provide transparency and support indexing. Reentrancy - Since execution can call external contracts, consider a reentrancy guard or ensure effects are applied after external calls.

On this page No headings found. In Soroban, performance isn't just about speed—it's about predictability and cost. Every operation (CPU instructions, memory allocation, and ledger access) consumes resources that are metered and capped. This playbook provides a repeatable, measurable workflow for optimizing your contracts. The Three Pillars of Cost CPU Instructions: The computational complexity of your logic. 2. RAM Usage: The memory peak during execution. 3. Storage (Footprint): The size and frequency of ledger reads and writes.

Optimization should never be "blind." Follow this cycle to ensure your efforts are targeted and effective: Measure (Baseline): Use soroban contract simulate to capture current resource usage. Analyze: Identify the bottleneck (e.g., is it high CPU or large storage reads?). Refactor: Apply a specific optimization technique. Verify: Re-measure and compare the delta.

Run your contract function through the CLI simulator to see the raw costs: soroban contract invoke \ --id <CONTRACT_ID> \ --source-account <ACCOUNT> \ --network <NETWORK> \ -- \ <FUNCTION_NAME> \ --arg1 <VALUE> Look for the Events or Simulation output, which includes: cpu_insns: Total CPU instructions. mem_limit: Peak memory usage. ledger_reads: Number of entries read. ledger_writes: Number of entries written.

To create reproducible results, you must control your environment. Stable Ledger State: Always run benchmarks against a known, pre-populated state. Release Profile: Always build your contract with cargo build --release before measuring. Warm vs. Cold Cache: Note that the first time an entry is read, it costs more than subsequent reads in the same transaction.

Every example contract in this repository ships a .wasm binary, and Soroban rejects contracts over 65,536 bytes (64 KiB). Size regressions are easy to introduce silently, so CI release-builds every example and fails when a binary exceeds its documented budget. Budgets live in examples/wasm-budgets.toml, as per-crate byte limits derived from release-baseline measurements. The check-wasm-budgets job runs bash scripts/check-wasm-budgets.sh, which release-builds each workspace member for the wasm32v1-none target (the current supported Soroban target; the legacy wasm32-unknown-unknown is rejected by soroban-sdk 27+ on modern Rust) and compares file size against the budget. Builds over budget exit non-zero, so the PR is blocked. The release profile is declared once at the workspace root (examples/Cargo.toml) with size-oriented settings (opt-level = "z", lto = true, strip = "symbols", panic = "abort"). Cargo only honors [profile.release] at the workspace root — per-package tables are silently ignored and would otherwise fall back to the size-inefficient default profile (no LTO, no stripping). Keeping it centralised means every example ships a small, stripped binary and the budgets below are measured against that same profile, which is exactly what gets deployed. The budget file is meant to be tight enough to catch regressions, not to pine a specific byte count. Each budget is the measured baseline plus ~25% headroom, so a meaningful regression tripping CI, while routine maintenance does not. If a contract genuinely needs more room after optimisation, raise its budget on the PR and explain why. Local validation: bash scripts/check-wasm-budgets.sh To refresh baselines after a deliberate, justified size change: cargo build --release --target wasm32v1-none --manifest-path examples/Cargo.toml find examples/target/wasm32v1-none/release -maxdepth 1 -name '*.wasm' -printf '%f %s\n' Then update wasm-budgets.toml with the new size + headroom and document the reason for the change.

Educational & Unaudited Examples The contract code snippets in this playbook are educational examples designed to demonstrate optimization techniques. They are unaudited and not production-ready. Production deployments must address key security and operational requirements: Authorization: These snippets omit require_auth() and caller verification for brevity. Real-world contracts must enforce explicit authorization on state-changing operations. Reentrancy: Although these snippets perform direct storage operations without external contract calls, any pattern involving external calls must consider state ordering and reentrancy protection. Storage TTL & Data Expiry: All Soroban storage entries are subject to Time-To-Live (TTL) expiration. Production contracts must implement a TTL management strategy (such as extend_ttl) to keep ledger entries active.

Problem: Iterating through a Vec stored in a single storage key to find or update an item. This is O(n) and becomes exponentially more expensive as the collection grows. Before (O(n)) After (O(1)) #[contracttype] pub struct Registry { pub users: Vec<Address>, } // Every time you add a user, you read the WHOLE list, // append, and write the WHOLE list back. pub fn add_user(env: Env, user: Address) { let mut registry: Registry = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::Reg).unwrap(); if !registry.users.contains(&user) { registry.users.push_back(user); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::Reg, &registry); } } // Use separate keys for each user. pub fn add_user(env: Env, user: Address) { let key = DataKey::User(user.clone()); if !env.storage().persistent().has(&key) { env.storage().persistent().set(&key, &true); } } Impact: Switching to individual keys reduces cpu_insns and ledger_read_bytes linearly with the size of the collection.

Problem: Storing all contract state in one large "monolithic" struct. Updating a single boolean requires reading and writing the entire 1KB+ object. Cost of Monoliths Reading a 2KB struct costs twice as much gas as reading a 1KB struct, even if you only need 1 byte of data from it. Optimization: Split the struct into "hot" (frequently updated) and "cold" (read-only or rarely updated) storage keys.

Problem: Accessing env.storage() multiple times for the same value in a single function call. // ❌ BAD: Multiple reads pub fn do_something(env: Env) { let admin = env.storage().instance().get::<_, Address>(&DataKey::Admin).unwrap(); // ... logic ... let admin_again = env.storage().instance().get::<_, Address>(&DataKey::Admin).unwrap(); } // ✅ GOOD: Read once, pass around pub fn do_something(env: Env) { let admin = env.storage().instance().get::<_, Address>(&DataKey::Admin).unwrap(); Self::internal_logic(&admin); }
If you need to store multiple flags or small numbers, pack them into a single u64 or u128 to save on storage bytes.

Instance Storage: Best for global config (read on every invocation). Persistent Storage: Best for user balances (long-lived, expensive). Temporary Storage: Best for oracles or sequence numbers (cheap, but must be bumped).

The project includes a compact benchmark contract at examples/tiny-contract to make bytecode-size work reproducible. It keeps the contract surface minimal while using a release profile tuned for size: [profile.release] opt-level = "z" panic = "abort" strip = "symbols" lto = true codegen-units = 1 Use the benchmark to compare a plain release build against a post-wasm-opt build: cargo build --manifest-path examples/tiny-contract/Cargo.toml --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --release stellar contract optimize \ --wasm examples/target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/tiny_contract.wasm \ --out examples/target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/tiny_contract.optimized.wasm

When submitting an optimization PR, include a "Before & After" table: Metric Before After Change CPU Instructions 1,200,000 450,000 -62.5% Mem Limit 512 KB 256 KB -50% Wasm Size 12 KB 9 KB -25% Ledger Reads 5 2 -60%

The oracle consumer pattern enables smart contracts to read external data (price feeds, asset prices, etc.) from trusted oracle contracts through cross-contract invocation.

An oracle consumer contract: Reads data from an external oracle contract Validates data freshness and accuracy Uses prices for calculations (value estimation, collateral checks) Handles oracle failures gracefully Maintains configurable trust parameters

DEX/AMM: Price feeds for token swaps and liquidity pools Lending Protocols: Collateral valuation and liquidation pricing Staking: Asset price feeds for reward calculations Insurance: Event triggers based on oracle data Derivatives: Price feeds for options and futures

┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ Oracle Consumer Contract │ ├─────────────────────────────┤ │ get_price(asset) │ │ get_price_data(asset) │ │ calculate_value(asset, amt) │ │ validate_freshness() │ └──────────┬──────────────────┘ │ Cross-Contract Call │ ┌──────────▼──────────────────┐ │ Oracle Contract │ ├─────────────────────────────┤ │ price_feeds (persistent) │ │ last_update (timestamp) │ │ update_prices() │ └─────────────────────────────┘

Query: Consumer asks oracle for price of asset Fetch: Oracle looks up price from data store Return: Oracle returns price with metadata (decimals, timestamp) Validate: Consumer checks freshness and accuracy Use: Consumer uses validated price for calculations
Oracle Contract: Deployed by trusted party Data Accuracy: Oracle is incentivized to provide accurate prices Timeliness: Oracle updates prices regularly Integrity: Oracle cannot be tampered with

Freshness Checks: Reject stale data beyond max_age Price Bounds: Reject prices outside reasonable ranges Multiple Oracles: Average prices from multiple sources Circuit Breakers: Pause operations if prices are unusual

Unaudited Educational Example This pattern and contract code are provided for educational purposes only. The code is unaudited and not intended for production use. Before deploying contracts handling real funds on mainnet, conduct thorough security reviews, write extensive tests, and obtain professional security audits.

#[contract] pub struct OracleConsumer; #[contractimpl] impl OracleConsumer { /// Initialize with oracle address and data freshness requirement pub fn init(env: Env, oracle_address: Address, max_age_secs: u64) { env.storage() .instance() .set(&symbol_short!("oracle"), &oracle_address); env.storage() .instance() .set(&symbol_short!("max_age"), &max_age_secs); } /// Fetch price from oracle with validation pub fn get_price(env: Env, asset: Symbol) -> Result<i128, OracleError> { let oracle = env.storage() .instance() .get(&symbol_short!("oracle")) .expect("Oracle not initialized"); // Call oracle contract let price_data: Vec<i128> = env .invoke_contract( &oracle, &symbol_short!("get_price"), soroban_sdk::vec![&env, asset.into_val(&env)], ) .map_err(|_| OracleError::InvalidOracle)?; // Validate response format if price_data.len() < 3 { return Err(OracleError::InvalidPrice); } let price = price_data.get_unchecked(0); let timestamp = price_data.get_unchecked(2) as u64; // Validate price is positive if price <= 0 { return Err(OracleError::InvalidPrice); } // Check data freshness let max_age = env.storage() .instance() .get(&symbol_short!("max_age")) .unwrap_or(3600); let current_time = env.ledger().timestamp(); let age = current_time.checked_sub(timestamp) .ok_or(OracleError::StaleData)?; if age > max_age { return Err(OracleError::StaleData); } Ok(price) } /// Calculate value of amount based on oracle price pub fn calculate_value( env: Env, asset: Symbol, amount: i128, ) -> Result<i128, OracleError> { let (price, decimals, _) = self.get_price_data(env, asset)?; // value = (amount * price) / 10^decimals let value = amount .checked_mul(price) .ok_or(OracleError::InvalidPrice)? .checked_div(10_i128.pow(decimals)) .ok_or(OracleError::InvalidPrice)?; Ok(value) } }

#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Debug)] #[repr(u32)] pub enum OracleError { StaleData = 1, // Data too old InvalidOracle = 2, // Oracle call failed InvalidPrice = 3, // Price is invalid Unauthorized = 4, // Not authorized }

The oracle consumer includes comprehensive tests with a mock oracle: #[contract] pub struct MockOracle; #[contractimpl] impl MockOracle { pub fn get_price(env: Env, asset: Symbol) -> Vec<i128> { // Return: [price, decimals, timestamp] soroban_sdk::vec![ &env, 1_000_000, // $1.00 6, // 6 decimals env.ledger().timestamp() as i128, // current time ] } } #[test] fn test_get_price() { let env = Env::default(); let consumer_id = env.register_contract(None, OracleConsumer); let oracle_id = env.register_contract(None, MockOracle); let client = OracleConsumerClient::new(&env, &consumer_id); client.init(&oracle_id, &3600); let price = client.get_price(&Symbol::new(&env, "USD")).unwrap(); assert_eq!(price, 1_000_000); } #[test] fn test_stale_data_rejection() { let env = Env::default(); // ... setup ... // Advance time beyond max_age env.ledger_mut().set_timestamp(old_timestamp + 7200); let result = client.get_price(&Symbol::new(&env, "USD")); assert_eq!(result, Err(OracleError::StaleData)); }
Always validate timestamp and reject stale data: let max_age = 3600; // 1 hour let age = current_time - timestamp; if age > max_age { return Err(OracleError::StaleData); }
Reject prices outside reasonable ranges: // BTC price between $10k and $100k if price < 10_000_000_000 || price > 100_000_000_000 { return Err(OracleError::InvalidPrice); }

Use multiple oracles to prevent single point of failure: pub fn get_median_price(env: Env, asset: Symbol) -> Result<i128, OracleError> { let mut prices = Vec::new(); for oracle_addr in self.get_oracles(&env)? { if let Ok(price) = self.fetch_from_oracle(&env, &oracle_addr, &asset) { prices.push(price); } } if prices.is_empty() { return Err(OracleError::InvalidOracle); } // Return median to handle outliers prices.sort(); Ok(prices[prices.len() / 2]) }

Handle oracle failures gracefully: pub fn get_price_or_cached( env: Env, asset: Symbol, ) -> Result<i128, OracleError> { // Try fresh price match self.get_price(&env, &asset) { Ok(price) => { // Cache for fallback self.cache_price(&env, &asset, price)?; Ok(price) } Err(_) => { // Fall back to cached price if oracle fails self.get_cached_price(&env, &asset) } } }

Restrict configuration changes to authorized addresses: pub fn set_oracle(env: Env, new_oracle: Address) { let admin: Address = env.storage() .instance() .get(&symbol_short!("admin")) .expect("Admin not set"); require_auth(&admin); env.storage() .instance() .set(&symbol_short!("oracle"), &new_oracle); }

Handle different decimal places: pub fn normalize_price(price: i128, decimals: u32, target_decimals: u32) -> i128 { if decimals > target_decimals { price / 10_i128.pow(decimals - target_decimals) } else { price * 10_i128.pow(target_decimals - decimals) } }

Calculate asset value from price and amount: pub fn calculate_usd_value( price: i128, // Price in USD decimals: u32, // Price decimals amount: i128, // Amount of asset amount_decimals: u32, // Asset decimals ) -> Result<i128, OracleError> { // Normalize to same decimal place let price_normalized = normalize_price(price, decimals, amount_decimals); // value = amount * price / 10^decimals let value = amount .checked_mul(price_normalized) .ok_or(OracleError::InvalidPrice)? .checked_div(10_i128.pow(amount_decimals)) .ok_or(OracleError::InvalidPrice)?; Ok(value) }

Pause operations if price changes dramatically: pub fn check_circuit_breaker( env: Env, asset: Symbol, new_price: i128, ) -> Result<(), OracleError> { let old_price = self.get_cached_price(&env, &asset)?; // Allow max 20% price change let max_deviation = old_price / 5; let deviation = (new_price as i128 - old_price).abs(); if deviation > max_deviation { return Err(OracleError::PriceDeviation); } Ok(()) }

Risk: Oracle goes offline, contract uses stale prices Mitigation: Set reasonable max_age (typically 1 hour) Monitor oracle update frequency Use circuit breakers for unusual price changes Fall back to cached prices
Risk: Oracle provides false prices Mitigation: Use multiple independent oracle sources Verify oracle is properly incentivized/bonded Implement price bounds checking Monitor for suspicious patterns

Risk: Malicious oracle contract returns crafted data Mitigation: Whitelist oracle addresses Validate response format and types Use safe math (checked_mul, checked_div) Test with multiple data scenarios
Risk: Oracle takes excessive gas or fails unexpectedly Mitigation: Set gas limits on oracle calls Implement timeouts Use try/catch for failure scenarios Fall back to cached prices

Risk: Storage entry expiration halting contract operations The consumer contract relies on env.storage().instance() to persist the oracle contract address and max_age threshold. In Soroban, all ledger entries (including contract instance storage) have a Time-To-Live (TTL) and will eventually expire if not extended. If instance storage expires, calls to get_price or calculate_value will fail when trying to load uninitialized or expired keys. Mitigation: Extend instance TTL during initialization or key configuration updates (env.storage().instance().extend_ttl(...)). Implement automated off-chain monitoring or bump operations using the Soroban CLI / SDK before TTL expiration occurs.

Risk: Cross-contract call reentrancy when querying oracle data The contract executes cross-contract invocations (env.invoke_contract) to fetch price data from the configured external oracle contract. In this specific implementation, get_price and get_price_data are read-only with respect to the consumer contract's internal state—they fetch external price vectors, validate timestamps, and return values without making prior or subsequent modifications to consumer storage. Because no state transitions occur around the cross-contract invocation in this example flow, classic reentrancy state manipulation does not directly affect this read-only pattern. However, if you integrate this oracle consumer into a larger contract protocol (such as a lending market or DEX) where oracle price fetches trigger state updates, collateral adjustments, or asset transfers, you must follow the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern or reentrancy guards to prevent untrusted external contracts from reentering state-modifying functions.

Trust Dependency: Consumer trusts oracle's data accuracy Availability: Relies on oracle being online Latency: Data is never completely real-time Cost: Oracle calls consume gas Manipulation: Oracles can be attacked or compromised Storage TTL Expiry: Instance storage entries expire if not maintained via TTL extension calls Reentrancy Context: While the read-only oracle fetch is non-state-modifying, integrating callers must handle cross-contract interaction ordering safely
