The oracle price source (producer) pattern describes how a trusted account publishes on-chain price data that other contracts can consume. It is the counterpart to the Oracle Consumer pattern, which explains how to read prices; this page explains how to publish them.

A price oracle source contract: Stores a price, a decimal scale, and a ledger timestamp for each asset. Restricts publishing to a single admin address (enforced via require_auth). Exposes prices in a Vec<i128> format compatible with oracle-consumer. Lets consumers enforce their own freshness policy via get_price_checked. Emits events so off-chain indexers can track every update.

┌──────────────────────────────────┐ │ Off-chain price bot / relayer │ └──────────────────┬───────────────┘ │ set_price(asset, price, decimals) ▼ ┌──────────────────────────────────┐ │ PriceOracle (this contract) │ ├──────────────────────────────────┤ │ storage: DataKey::Price(asset) │ │ → PriceEntry { price, │ │ decimals, │ │ timestamp } │ ├──────────────────────────────────┤ │ get_price(asset) │◄── oracle-consumer (cross-contract) │ get_price_entry(asset) │◄── any contract │ get_price_checked(asset, age) │◄── any contract └──────────────────────────────────┘

/// Full price record stored for every asset. pub struct PriceEntry { /// Price scaled by 10^decimals. pub price: i128, /// Decimal places (0–18). pub decimals: u32, /// Ledger timestamp when the entry was written (seconds since Unix epoch). pub timestamp: u64, } The price field is an integer scaled by 10^decimals. A BTC price of $43,000.000000 with 6 decimal places is stored as 43_000_000_000.

Educational & Unaudited Example This pattern and its reference implementation are provided for educational purposes only. The contract code has not been audited and is not production-ready. Users must perform an appropriate security review and independent audit before deploying any contract handling real funds to a live network. Contract Tests #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{ contract, contracterror, contractimpl, contracttype, symbol_short, Address, Env, Symbol, }; #[contracterror] #[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Debug)] #[repr(u32)] pub enum OracleError { Unauthorized = 1, AssetNotFound = 2, StalePrice = 3, InvalidArgument = 4, NotInitialized = 5, } #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone)] pub enum DataKey { Admin, Price(Symbol), } #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] pub struct PriceEntry { pub price: i128, pub decimals: u32, pub timestamp: u64, } #[contract] pub struct PriceOracle; #[contractimpl] impl PriceOracle { /// Initialise with an admin address (callable once). pub fn init(env: Env, admin: Address) { if env.storage().instance().has(&DataKey::Admin) { panic!("already initialized"); } env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::Admin, &admin); } /// Return the current admin. pub fn get_admin(env: Env) -> Result<Address, OracleError> { env.storage() .instance() .get(&DataKey::Admin) .ok_or(OracleError::NotInitialized) } /// Transfer admin rights (current admin must sign). pub fn set_admin(env: Env, new_admin: Address) -> Result<(), OracleError> { let admin = Self::require_admin(&env)?; admin.require_auth(); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::Admin, &new_admin); Ok(()) } /// Publish or update a price (admin-only). /// /// * `asset` – asset identifier, e.g. `Symbol::new(&env, "BTC")` /// * `price` – must be > 0 /// * `decimals` – 0–18 pub fn set_price( env: Env, asset: Symbol, price: i128, decimals: u32, ) -> Result<(), OracleError> { let admin = Self::require_admin(&env)?; admin.require_auth(); // ← admin must sign every price update if price <= 0 || decimals > 18 { return Err(OracleError::InvalidArgument); } let entry = PriceEntry { price, decimals, timestamp: env.ledger().timestamp(), }; env.storage() .persistent() .set(&DataKey::Price(asset.clone()), &entry); env.events().publish( (symbol_short!("set_price"), asset), (price, decimals, entry.timestamp), ); Ok(()) } /// Raw entry without freshness check. pub fn get_price_entry(env: Env, asset: Symbol) -> Result<PriceEntry, OracleError> { env.storage() .persistent() .get(&DataKey::Price(asset)) .ok_or(OracleError::AssetNotFound) } /// Flat Vec<i128> compatible with oracle-consumer's expected format: /// `[price, decimals, timestamp]`. pub fn get_price( env: Env, asset: Symbol, ) -> Result<soroban_sdk::Vec<i128>, OracleError> { let entry: PriceEntry = env .storage() .persistent() .get(&DataKey::Price(asset)) .ok_or(OracleError::AssetNotFound)?; Ok(soroban_sdk::vec![ &env, entry.price, entry.decimals as i128, entry.timestamp as i128, ]) } /// Freshness-checked read: returns StalePrice when age > max_age_secs. pub fn get_price_checked( env: Env, asset: Symbol, max_age_secs: u64, ) -> Result<PriceEntry, OracleError> { let entry: PriceEntry = env .storage() .persistent() .get(&DataKey::Price(asset)) .ok_or(OracleError::AssetNotFound)?; let age = env .ledger() .timestamp() .checked_sub(entry.timestamp) .ok_or(OracleError::StalePrice)?; if age > max_age_secs { return Err(OracleError::StalePrice); } Ok(entry) } fn require_admin(env: &Env) -> Result<Address, OracleError> { env.storage() .instance() .get(&DataKey::Admin) .ok_or(OracleError::NotInitialized) } } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; let id = env.register(PriceOracle, ()); let client = PriceOracleClient::new(&env, &id); client.init(&admin); (env, admin, client) } // ── Admin-only set_price ──────────────────────────────────────────────── #[test] fn test_set_price_succeeds_for_admin() { let (env, _, client) = setup(); let asset = Symbol::new(&env, "BTC"); client.set_price(&asset, &43_000_000_000_i128, &6); let entry = client.get_price_entry(&asset); assert_eq!(entry.price, 43_000_000_000_i128); assert_eq!(entry.decimals, 6); } #[test] fn test_set_price_requires_admin_auth() { // No mock_all_auths → real auth is enforced. let env = Env::default(); let admin = Address::generate(&env); let id = env.register(PriceOracle, ()); let client = PriceOracleClient::new(&env, &id); env.mock_all_auths(); client.init(&admin); // Auth mock removed — non-admin attempt must fail. let result = client .try_set_price(&Symbol::new(&env, "BTC"), &1_000_i128, &6); assert!(result.is_err()); } #[test] fn test_set_price_rejects_zero() { let (env, _, client) = setup(); let result = client .try_set_price(&Symbol::new(&env, "BTC"), &0_i128, &6); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(OracleError::InvalidArgument))); } #[test] fn test_set_price_rejects_negative() { let (env, _, client) = setup(); let result = client .try_set_price(&Symbol::new(&env, "BTC"), &-1_i128, &6); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(OracleError::InvalidArgument))); } #[test] fn test_set_price_rejects_decimals_above_18() { let (env, _, client) = setup(); let result = client .try_set_price(&Symbol::new(&env, "BTC"), &1_000_i128, &19); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(OracleError::InvalidArgument))); } // ── Stale price rejection ────────────────────────────────────────────── #[test] fn test_stale_price_rejected() { let (env, _, client) = setup(); let asset = Symbol::new(&env, "USD"); client.set_price(&asset, &1_000_000_i128, &6); // Advance ledger 2 hours; max_age is 1 hour. env.ledger().with_mut(|i| i.timestamp += 7_200); let result = client.try_get_price_checked(&asset, &3600_u64); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(OracleError::StalePrice))); } #[test] fn test_fresh_price_accepted() { let (env, _, client) = setup(); let asset = Symbol::new(&env, "USD"); client.set_price(&asset, &1_000_000_i128, &6); // Advance exactly max_age → still valid. env.ledger().with_mut(|i| i.timestamp += 3_600); let entry = client.get_price_checked(&asset, &3_600_u64); assert_eq!(entry.price, 1_000_000_i128); } // ── get_price Vec format (oracle-consumer compatibility) ─────────────── #[test] fn test_get_price_vec_format() { let (env, _, client) = setup(); let asset = Symbol::new(&env, "ETH"); client.set_price(&asset, &2_000_000_000_i128, &6); let data = client.get_price(&asset); assert_eq!(data.len(), 3); assert_eq!(data.get_unchecked(0), 2_000_000_000_i128); // price assert_eq!(data.get_unchecked(1), 6_i128); // decimals assert!(data.get_unchecked(2) >= 0); // timestamp } }

The oracle writes the current ledger timestamp (env.ledger().timestamp()) into every PriceEntry. Consumers compare this against the current ledger time: age = now − entry.timestamp if age > max_age_secs → reject (StalePrice) The boundary is inclusive: age == max_age_secs is still valid. One second past the boundary is stale. This is a deliberate separation of concerns: the oracle does not know what freshness a given consumer requires, so consumers pass their own max_age on every call.

get_price(asset) returns Vec<i128> with exactly three elements: Index Value 0 price 1 decimals (cast to i128) 2 timestamp (cast to i128) This matches what oracle-consumer expects when calling env.invoke_contract(&oracle, &symbol_short!("get_price"), ...). Pointing the consumer's oracle_address at a deployed price-oracle instance requires no changes to the consumer contract.

set_price (and set_admin) require admin.require_auth(). The Soroban SDK will reject the transaction unless the admin address has signed it. In tests, wrap the setup in env.mock_all_auths() but remove the mock for tests that explicitly verify the rejection path. // Test that a non-admin cannot publish a price: let env = Env::default(); // ... init with mock_all_auths ... // After init, auth is no longer mocked. let result = client.try_set_price(&asset, &price, &decimals); assert!(result.is_err()); // ← auth failure

Use persistent storage for prices – price entries must survive ledger expiry. The admin address can use instance storage because the contract itself keeps it alive. Manage storage TTLs – persistent storage entries have a finite TTL in Soroban. Off-chain price bots or maintenance operations should extend (bump) entry TTLs regularly so consumers do not encounter AssetNotFound due to entry expiration. Validate all inputs in set_price – check that price > 0 and decimals ≤ 18 before writing to storage. Malformed entries cannot be unset without a subsequent valid set_price call. Emit an event on every update – the set_price event lets off-chain monitors and indexers build a complete price history without polling contract state. Keep decimals consistent – choose a fixed decimal scale per asset and document it. Changing decimals across updates will confuse consumers that cache the scale. Rotate the admin key periodically – use set_admin to rotate the admin to a new key if the current key is compromised.

Risk Mitigation Admin key compromise Rotate via set_admin; consider multi-sig admin Stale prices used downstream Consumers call get_price_checked with tight max_age Storage entry expiration Off-chain bots periodically extend (bump) persistent price entry TTLs Integer overflow in price arithmetic Use checked_mul / checked_div in consumers Deployment to wrong network Verify contract address in consumer before deploying

Traditional reentrancy attacks do not apply to this PriceOracle pattern. The contract's mutating functions (init, set_admin, and set_price) modify state directly without invoking external contracts. Furthermore, Soroban's execution environment enforces single-threaded host-level execution per contract invocation unless control is explicitly handed off through cross-contract calls. Because this contract makes no external calls during state updates, state cannot be manipulated mid-execution by a re-entrant caller.

Soroban uses a rent-based state model where all storage entries have a Time-To-Live (TTL): Persistent Storage: Price records written via env.storage().persistent() will expire if their TTL lapses without renewal. If a price entry expires, subsequent calls to get_price, get_price_entry, or get_price_checked will return OracleError::AssetNotFound. Instance Storage: The admin address stored in env.storage().instance() shares the lifetime of the contract instance. If the instance TTL expires, administrative functions (set_price, set_admin) will fail until the instance is restored. Operational Requirement: Price relayers or automated off-chain services must manage storage TTL extensions (e.g. extending key TTLs during routine price updates) as an operational requirement.

The simple-dao example uses a clear, auditable state machine so that proposals can only advance through valid transitions. This pattern encodes the full lifecycle as a #[contracttype] enum and enforces transitions at the contract boundary, making invalid states unrepresentable on-chain. Pending ──► Active ──► Succeeded ──► Executed └──► Defeated Pending ──► Cancelled Prerequisites Rust stable and cargo Soroban CLI installed (setup guide) Familiarity with contracttype enums and instance storage Implementation Educational & Unaudited Example This pattern and its code examples are provided for educational purposes only and have not been security audited. Do not deploy or adapt this code directly in production environments without independent security reviews and comprehensive testing. Reentrancy Limitations: The illustrative contract below operates synchronously without external contract calls. However, production governance contracts (such as the full simple-dao example) that execute external calls during proposal execution must account for reentrancy and control-flow implications, ensuring state updates occur prior to external invocations or using reentrancy guards. Storage TTL & Data Expiry: The example relies on Soroban instance storage (env.storage().instance()), which is subject to ledger time-to-live (TTL) and data expiration. The example does not demonstrate TTL extension (extend_ttl). Production implementations must account for storage rent management so proposal state and voting data do not expire unexpectedly during active governance lifecycles. Design principle Encode every invalid state as a compile-time impossibility or a guarded assert!. Never rely on callers to pass the right state — the contract should enforce it. Contract Tests #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, contracttype, Env}; /// All valid proposal states. #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone, PartialEq, Debug)] pub enum ProposalState { Pending, // created but voting not open Active, // voting is open Succeeded, // more for-votes than against Defeated, // equal or more against-votes Cancelled, // proposer withdrew before voting opened Executed, // on-chain action has been carried out } #[contracttype] pub enum DataKey { State, VotesFor, VotesAgainst, } #[contract] pub struct SimpleDao; #[contractimpl] impl SimpleDao { /// Create a new proposal in the Pending state. pub fn create(env: Env) { env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::State, &ProposalState::Pending); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::VotesFor, &0_u32); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::VotesAgainst, &0_u32); } /// Pending → Active: open voting. pub fn activate(env: Env) { let state: ProposalState = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::State).unwrap(); assert!(state == ProposalState::Pending, "must be Pending to activate"); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::State, &ProposalState::Active); } /// Pending → Cancelled: withdraw the proposal before voting opens. pub fn cancel(env: Env) { let state: ProposalState = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::State).unwrap(); assert!(state == ProposalState::Pending, "must be Pending to cancel"); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::State, &ProposalState::Cancelled); } /// Record a vote while Active. pub fn vote(env: Env, in_favor: bool) { let state: ProposalState = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::State).unwrap(); assert!(state == ProposalState::Active, "voting is not open"); if in_favor { let v: u32 = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::VotesFor).unwrap_or(0); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::VotesFor, &(v + 1)); } else { let v: u32 = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::VotesAgainst).unwrap_or(0); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::VotesAgainst, &(v + 1)); } } /// Active → Succeeded or Defeated based on vote counts. pub fn finalize(env: Env) { let state: ProposalState = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::State).unwrap(); assert!(state == ProposalState::Active, "must be Active to finalize"); let for_votes: u32 = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::VotesFor).unwrap_or(0); let against_votes: u32 = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::VotesAgainst).unwrap_or(0); let next = if for_votes > against_votes { ProposalState::Succeeded } else { ProposalState::Defeated }; env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::State, &next); } /// Succeeded → Executed: carry out the on-chain action. pub fn execute(env: Env) { let state: ProposalState = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::State).unwrap(); assert!(state == ProposalState::Succeeded, "must be Succeeded to execute"); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::State, &ProposalState::Executed); } /// Get the current proposal state. pub fn get_state(env: Env) -> ProposalState { env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::State).unwrap() } } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; use soroban_sdk::Env; fn setup() -> (Env, soroban_sdk::Address) { let env = Env::default(); let id = env.register(SimpleDao, ()); (env, id) } #[test] fn test_create_sets_pending() { let (env, id) = setup(); let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); assert_eq!(client.get_state(), ProposalState::Pending); } #[test] fn test_pending_to_active() { let (env, id) = setup(); let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); client.activate(); assert_eq!(client.get_state(), ProposalState::Active); } #[test] fn test_active_to_succeeded() { let (env, id) = setup(); let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); client.activate(); client.vote(&true); client.vote(&true); client.vote(&false); client.finalize(); assert_eq!(client.get_state(), ProposalState::Succeeded); } #[test] fn test_active_to_defeated() { let (env, id) = setup(); let client = SimpleDaoClient::new(&env, &id); client.create(); client.activate(); client.vote(&false); client.vote(&false); client.vote(&true); client.finalize(); assert_eq!(client.get_state(), ProposalState::Defeated); Do not deploy or adapt this code directly in production environments without independent security reviews and comprehensive testing. Reentrancy Limitations: The illustrative contract below operates synchronously without external contract calls. However, production governance contracts (such as the full simple-dao example) that execute external calls during proposal execution must account for reentrancy and control-flow implications, ensuring state updates occur prior to external invocations or using reentrancy guards. Storage TTL & Data Expiry: The example relies on Soroban instance storage (env.storage().instance()), which is subject to ledger time-to-live (TTL) and data expiration. The example does not demonstrate TTL extension (extend_ttl). Production implementations must account for storage rent management so proposal state and voting data do not expire unexpectedly during active governance lifecycles. Design principle Encode every invalid state as a compile-time impossibility or a guarded assert!. Never rely on callers to pass the right state — the contract should enforce it. env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::VotesAgainst, &0_u32); } /// Pending → Active: open voting. pub fn activate(env: Env) { let state: ProposalState = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::State).unwrap(); assert!(state == ProposalState::Pending, "must be Pending to activate"); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::State, &ProposalState::Active); } /// Pending → Cancelled: withdraw the proposal before voting opens. pub fn cancel(env: Env) { let state: ProposalState = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::State).unwrap(); A pull payment inverts the direction of a payout: instead of a contract pushing tokens to a receiver during an external call, it merely records a credit for the beneficiary, who then calls withdraw to pull the funds whenever they choose. This pattern mitigates two failure classes in push-style payout contracts: Failed downstream transfers — if the pushed transfer reverts, the whole transaction reverts and the payout may be stuck or need to be re-run. With a pull payment the credit is recorded first and funds are drawn on demand. Reentrancy — because the credit is zeroed in storage before the external token transfer (Checks-Effects-Interactions), a re-entering call sees a zero balance and cannot double-spend. It is a natural complement to the Reentrancy Guard Pattern: the guard blocks re-entrant calls with a mutex, while pull payments remove the vulnerable interaction window altogether. Prerequisites Rust and soroban-sdk version 27+ Familiarity with token contract clients (token::Client, StellarAssetClient) Understanding of the Checks-Effects-Interactions ordering Familiarity with the Reentrancy Guard Pattern Goals Credit a beneficiary in storage without transferring tokens at release time. Allow a beneficiary to pull their credited payment in a single authorized call. Demonstrate Checks-Effects-Interactions by zeroing the credit before the transfer. Prove, under test, that the credit is zeroed before the transfer and cannot be double-spent. Implementation Storage Keys and Errors​ An Owner controls crediting, and a Credit(Address) mapping holds each beneficiary's unwithdrawn balance. The token address is stored in instance storage. #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone)] pub enum DataKey { Owner, Credit(Address), } #[contracterror] #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq, PartialOrd, Ord)] #[repr(u32)] pub enum Error { Unauthorized = 1, InvalidAmount = 2, InsufficientCredit = 3, TransferFailed = 4, } Initialize​ Store the payout owner and the payout token. The instance-storage owner acts as the authorization gate for credit_payment. pub fn init(env: Env, owner: Address, token: Address) { if env.storage().instance().has(&DataKey::Owner) { panic!("already initialized"); } env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::Owner, &owner); env.storage() .instance() .set(&Symbol::new(&env, "Token"), &token); } Credit (No Transfer)​ credit_payment only mutates storage — no token transfer occurs here, which is exactly what makes a failed downstream payout impossible. pub fn credit_payment(env: Env, beneficiary: Address, amount: i128) -> Result<(), Error> { Self::require_owner(&env)?; if amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } let current = Self::credit(env.clone(), beneficiary.clone()); let new = current.checked_add(amount).expect("credit overflow"); env.storage() .persistent() .set(&DataKey::Credit(beneficiary), &new); Ok(()) } Withdraw (Checks-Effects-Interactions)​ The withdrawal is ordered deliberately: Checks — authenticate the beneficiary and validate the amount against the credit. Effects — zero (or reduce) the credit in storage before any interaction. Interactions — perform the token transfer last. pub fn withdraw(env: Env, beneficiary: Address, amount: i128) -> Result<(), Error> { beneficiary.require_auth(); // ── Checks ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── if amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } let credited = Self::credit(env.clone(), beneficiary.clone()); if credited < amount { return Err(Error::InsufficientCredit); } // ── Effects ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── // Zero the credit before any interaction (checks-effects-interactions). let remaining = credited - amount; if remaining > 0 { env.storage() .persistent() .set(&DataKey::Credit(beneficiary.clone()), &remaining); } else { env.storage() .persistent() .remove(&DataKey::Credit(beneficiary.clone())); } // ── Interactions ────────────────────────────────────────────────── let token_address = Self::token(env.clone()); token::Client::new(&env, &token_address).transfer( &env.current_contract_address(), &beneficiary, &amount, ); Ok(()) } Zeroing the credit before the transfer means a reverting or re-entered transfer can never be used to withdraw the same funds twice. Security Considerations Zero before transfer — always clear the credit in storage before the token transfer. This is the crux of Checks-Effects-Interactions for payouts. Authorize withdrawals — beneficiary.require_auth() ensures only the credited account can pull its payment. Gate crediting — only the Owner stored at init may credit_payment, preventing arbitrary inflation of credits. Validate amounts — reject non-positive amounts and amounts exceeding the credited balance. Relationship to reentrancy — pull payments reduce the interaction surface; combine with a reentrancy guard when you still perform external calls elsewhere. Tests The example verifies the credit round trip, that the credit is zeroed before transfer, partial withdrawals, and that over-withdrawals are rejected without state changes. #[test] fn test_credit_and_withdraw_round_trip() { let (_env, owner, beneficiary, token_id, contract) = setup(); contract.credit_payment(&beneficiary, &1_000); assert_eq!(contract.credit(&beneficiary), 1_000); contract.withdraw(&beneficiary, &1_000); assert_eq!(contract.credit(&beneficiary), 0); } #[test] fn test_withdraw_more_than_credit_fails() { let (_env, _owner, beneficiary, _token_id, contract) = setup(); contract.credit_payment(&beneficiary, &100); let res = contract.try_withdraw(&beneficiary, &200); assert_eq!(res.unwrap_err().unwrap(), Error::InsufficientCredit); // Credit unchanged because the check failed before any effects. assert_eq!(contract.credit(&beneficiary), 100); } Full Example The complete tested implementation is available in the repository: examples/pull-payment

A soulbound token (SBT) is a non-transferable token permanently bound to a single holder address from the moment it is minted. Unlike standard ERC-20-like tokens, soulbound tokens cannot be bought, sold, or delegated — they represent intrinsic properties of an account rather than a tradable asset. When to use Use this pattern when you need on-chain credentials, badges, or attestations that must remain with their original recipient. If you need freely transferable tokens, see the Basic Token pattern or examples/token-transfer/ for an ERC-20-style implementation with allowances.

Use-case Example Verifiable credentials KYC attestation, academic certificate Achievement badges "First 100 contributors" milestone Membership records DAO membership, on-chain passport Access passes Permissioned, non-tradable access tokens Reputation scores Weighted contribution points Prerequisites Rust stable and cargo Soroban CLI installed (setup guide) Familiarity with Soroban contracts and soroban_sdk Understanding of Address types, authentication, and require_auth() Implementation The contract exposes the standard token metadata interface (name, symbol, decimals) but overrides transfer and transfer_from to always fail with the TransferNotAllowed contract error, enforcing non-transferability at the contract level. Only the stored admin may mint new tokens or burn (revoke) existing ones. ⚠️ Disclaimer: Un-audited Example This contract is provided for educational purposes only and has not been audited. Do NOT use in production or with real funds. No reentrancy concerns apply – the contract does not expose any mutable entry points that could be re‑entered. Storage entries persist indefinitely; there is no automatic TTL or data‑expiry mechanism. Contract Tests Running Tests #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{ contract, contracterror, contractimpl, contracttype, panic_with_error, symbol_short, Address, Env, String, Symbol, }; /// Storage keys used by the soulbound token. #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone)] pub enum DataKey { Balance(Address), Admin, TotalSupply, Name, Symbol, Decimals, } /// Error codes surfaced by the soulbound token contract. #[contracterror] #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq, PartialOrd, Ord)] #[repr(u32)] pub enum Error { Unauthorized = 1, InvalidAmount = 2, InsufficientBalance = 3, AlreadyInitialized = 4, TransferNotAllowed = 5, } #[contract] pub struct SoulboundToken; #[contractimpl] impl SoulboundToken { fn get_admin(env: &Env) -> Address { env.storage() .persistent() .get(&DataKey::Admin) .expect("soulbound: contract not initialized") } fn require_admin(env: &Env, caller: &Address) { let admin = Self::get_admin(env); if *caller != admin { panic_with_error!(env, Error::Unauthorized); } caller.require_auth(); } /// Initialize the token once. Stores admin address and token metadata. pub fn initialize( env: Env, admin: Address, name: String, symbol: String, decimals: u32, ) -> Result<(), Error> { if env.storage().persistent().has(&DataKey::Admin) { return Err(Error::AlreadyInitialized); } admin.require_auth(); env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Admin, &admin); env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Name, &name); env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Symbol, &symbol); env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Decimals, &decimals); env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::TotalSupply, &0_i128); env.events().publish( (Symbol::new(&env, "initialize"),), (admin, name, symbol, decimals), ); Ok(()) } /// Admin-only: mint soulbound tokens to `to`. pub fn mint(env: Env, admin: Address, to: Address, amount: i128) -> Result<(), Error> { if amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } Self::require_admin(&env, &admin); let balance_key = DataKey::Balance(to.clone()); let current: i128 = env.storage().persistent().get(&balance_key).unwrap_or(0); env.storage().persistent().set(&balance_key, &(current + amount)); let supply: i128 = env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::TotalSupply).unwrap_or(0); env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::TotalSupply, &(supply + amount)); env.events().publish((symbol_short!("mint"), to), (admin, amount)); Ok(()) } /// DISABLED — soulbound tokens cannot be transferred. /// /// The call always fails with `Error::TransferNotAllowed`. There is no bypass, allowance, or admin override for transfers. Clients receive a descriptive contract error rather than a silent no-op. Admin Authorization​ Every mutating operation (mint, burn) requires both: Identity check: the admin argument must equal the stored admin address. Signature check: admin.require_auth() verifies the caller's cryptographic signature in the Soroban auth framework. fn require_admin(env: &Env, caller: &Address) { let admin = Self::get_admin(env); if *caller != admin { panic_with_error!(env, Error::Unauthorized); // identity mismatch } caller.require_auth(); // cryptographic proof } Burn as Revocation​ burn allows the admin to reduce a holder's balance, effectively revoking a credential. This is useful when a certification expires or a badge was issued in error. After burning, the holder's balance decreases and the total supply shrinks. Unaudited example — not for production This pattern is an educational example. The copy-paste contract logic and supporting snippets are not audited, are not a production-governance model, and should not be deployed with real funds or user assets. This page demonstrates the mechanics of continuous accrual and withdrawable balances, not a full production security review. The core flow here is not reentrancy-sensitive by itself because it computes available amounts from stored state and does not invoke another contract during the withdrawal path. If you adapt this pattern to call external contracts or custom tokens during settlement, treat that variation as reentrancy-sensitive and apply the same protections as the dedicated reentrancy-guard pattern. Storage lifetime is also finite in Soroban. Persistent entries age out unless their TTL is extended, while temporary entries are deleted when expired. For long-lived stream state, make sure your contract explicitly manages TTL and archival behavior; network minimums are roughly min_persistent_entry_ttl ≈ 4,096 ledgers and min_temp_entry_ttl ≈ 16 ledgers, with a practical upper extension cap around max_entry_ttl ≈ 6,312,000 ledgers. A streaming payment contract allows tokens to accrue linearly over time, with the recipient able to withdraw the currently available portion at any time. This pattern is useful for payroll, subscriptions, vesting without cliffs, and other scenarios where value transfers continuously.

Unlike token vesting (which typically releases tokens at milestones or with a cliff), streaming payments continuously accrue balance. The recipient can withdraw repeatedly without waiting for a single release event.

StreamPayment Contract ├── initialize(sender, recipient, token, total_amount, end_time) ├── withdraw() -> amount ├── available_amount() -> amount ├── stream() -> Stream └── withdrawable_at(stream, timestamp) -> amount

pub struct Stream { pub sender: Address, // Who funded the stream pub recipient: Address, // Who can withdraw pub token: Address, // Stellar asset contract pub start_time: u64, // When the stream begins pub end_time: u64, // When full amount is available pub total_amount: i128, // Total tokens deposited pub withdrawn_amount: i128, // Tokens already withdrawn }

The withdrawable amount at any timestamp is calculated as: pub fn withdrawable_at(stream: &Stream, timestamp: u64) -> Result<i128, Error> { if timestamp < stream.start_time { return Ok(0); } let total_released = if timestamp >= stream.end_time { stream.total_amount } else { let elapsed = i128::from(timestamp - stream.start_time); let duration = i128::from(stream.end_time - stream.start_time); stream.total_amount.checked_mul(elapsed).map(|a| a / duration)? }; let available = total_released.checked_sub(stream.withdrawn_amount)?; Ok(available) }

Before start: withdrawable = 0 During stream: withdrawable = total * elapsed / duration - withdrawn At/after end: withdrawable = total - withdrawn Never exceeds total: The contract prevents over-withdrawal

Soroban Token Interface Time and Scheduling Storage Concepts

A timelock vault locks an asset amount on-chain until a specific Unix timestamp. Only after that timestamp can the beneficiary withdraw the funds. The depositor may cancel before unlock to recover their assets.
Vesting schedules (e.g. lock team tokens for 12 months) Escrow with a time-based release trigger Scheduled payments / grant disbursements Time-delayed multi-sig safety nets

deposit(depositor, beneficiary, amount, unlock_time) └─ stores vault data; reverts if already initialised or inputs invalid withdraw() └─ releases funds to beneficiary; reverts if still locked or already claimed cancel() └─ depositor reclaims funds; only valid before unlock_time unlock_time() / amount() / beneficiary() / time_remaining() / is_claimed() └─ read-only view helpers

Key Type Storage Description Depositor Address persistent Account that locked the funds Beneficiary Address persistent Account allowed to withdraw after lock Amount i128 persistent Token amount locked (stroops) UnlockTime u64 persistent Unix timestamp (seconds) for release Claimed bool persistent Whether vault has been claimed/cancelled persistent storage ensures the vault survives ledger TTL expiry without manual extension.

Unaudited teaching example — Not for production The contract below is an unaudited educational example. It has not undergone an independent security review and is not fit for production or custodying real funds. It is designed solely to demonstrate time-based release and persistent storage mechanics in Soroban. Before copying or adapting this pattern, understand its key limits: Reentrancy limits: As written, reentrancy does not apply to this contract because none of deposit, withdraw, or cancel invokes external contracts, token contracts, or external callbacks. Soroban executes contract invocations to completion atomically by default. However, if this contract is extended to transfer actual tokens (such as via the Stellar Asset Contract or SEP-41 tokens), external calls can introduce reentrancy attack surfaces. Even though this contract enforces a checks-effects pattern (setting Claimed = true before returning values), external transfers should always follow state mutations or use a reentrancy guard. See Reentrancy limits. Token transfer omission: This contract only records numerical amounts and status flags in persistent storage; it does not custody or transfer real tokens. Real-world vaults must integrate SAC or custom token transfer clients with proper authorization. Storage TTL: While persistent storage is used so vault state is decoupled from the contract instance, persistent entries still have a ledger TTL and must be extended or restored if idle for extended periods. examples/timelock-vault/src/lib.rs #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contracterror, contractimpl, contracttype, Address, Env}; #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone)] pub enum DataKey { Depositor, Beneficiary, Amount, UnlockTime, Claimed, } #[contracterror] #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq, PartialOrd, Ord)] #[repr(u32)] pub enum Error { AlreadyInitialised = 1, NotInitialised = 2, NotUnlockedYet = 3, AlreadyClaimed = 4, Unauthorised = 5, InvalidAmount = 6, InvalidUnlockTime = 7, } #[contract] pub struct TimelockVault; #[contractimpl] impl TimelockVault { pub fn deposit( env: Env, depositor: Address, beneficiary: Address, amount: i128, unlock_time: u64, ) -> Result<(), Error> { depositor.require_auth(); if env.storage().persistent().has(&DataKey::Depositor) { return Err(Error::AlreadyInitialised); } if amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } if unlock_time <= env.ledger().timestamp() { return Err(Error::InvalidUnlockTime); } env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Depositor, &depositor); env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Beneficiary, &beneficiary); env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Amount, &amount); env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::UnlockTime, &unlock_time); env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Claimed, &false); Ok(()) } pub fn withdraw(env: Env) -> Result<i128, Error> { Self::assert_initialised(&env)?; if env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::Claimed).unwrap_or(false) { return Err(Error::AlreadyClaimed); } let unlock_time: u64 = env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::UnlockTime).unwrap(); if env.ledger().timestamp() < unlock_time { return Err(Error::NotUnlockedYet); } let amount: i128 = env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::Amount).unwrap(); env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Claimed, &true); Ok(amount) } pub fn cancel(env: Env) -> Result<i128, Error> { Self::assert_initialised(&env)?; let depositor: Address = env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::Depositor).unwrap(); depositor.require_auth(); if env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::Claimed).unwrap_or(false) { return Err(Error::AlreadyClaimed); } let unlock_time: u64 = env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::UnlockTime).unwrap(); if env.ledger().timestamp() >= unlock_time { return Err(Error::Unauthorised); } let amount: i128 = env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::Amount).unwrap(); env.storage().persistent().set(&DataKey::Claimed, &true); Ok(amount) } pub fn unlock_time(env: Env) -> Result<u64, Error> { Self::assert_initialised(&env)?; Ok(env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::UnlockTime).unwrap()) } pub fn amount(env: Env) -> Result<i128, Error> { Self::assert_initialised(&env)?; Ok(env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::Amount).unwrap()) } pub fn is_claimed(env: Env) -> bool { env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::Claimed).unwrap_or(false) } pub fn beneficiary(env: Env) -> Result<Address, Error> { Self::assert_initialised(&env)?; Ok(env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::Beneficiary).unwrap()) } pub fn time_remaining(env: Env) -> Result<u64, Error> { Self::assert_initialised(&env)?; let unlock_time: u64 = env.storage().persistent().get(&DataKey::UnlockTime).unwrap(); let now = env.ledger().timestamp(); Ok(if now >= unlock_time { 0 } else { unlock_time - now }) } fn assert_initialised(env: &Env) -> Result<(), Error> { if !env.storage().persistent().has(&DataKey::Depositor) { return Err(Error::NotInitialised); } Ok(()) } }

Claimed is set to true before returning the amount in both withdraw and cancel. This prevents re-entrancy even though Soroban's execution model already guards against it at the host level — the pattern makes the intent explicit. Why reentrancy does not apply as written: deposit, withdraw, and cancel only perform internal persistent storage reads and writes (env.storage().persistent()). No external cross-contract calls, callbacks, or token transfer invocations are performed. Without external contract invocations, untrusted code cannot regain control mid-execution. Limits when extending to real asset transfers: If you extend withdraw or cancel to call an external token contract (such as calling token::Client::new(&env, &token_address).transfer(...)), an external call runs before transaction finalization. Adhering to the checks-effects pattern shown here—marking Claimed = true in storage before initiating any external transfer—ensures that an attacker cannot perform a reentrant withdrawal even if a malicious contract receives execution flow. For complex multi-asset distributions or hooks, implement an explicit reentrancy lock using the Reentrancy Guard pattern.
Vault state must survive beyond a single ledger bump window. persistent storage entries have an independent TTL that can be extended, making them appropriate for long-duration locks (months/years).

cancel calls depositor.require_auth() so the depositor's signature must be present in the transaction's authorisation tree. This prevents a third party from prematurely cancelling a vault on behalf of the depositor.

This contract records amounts but does not move tokens directly — it is intentionally scoped as a basic vault to demonstrate the time-lock pattern without the additional complexity of SAC (Stellar Asset Contract) integration. See the token-transfer example for cross-contract token movement.

A token vesting contract lets a funder deposit a full token allocation up front and then release only the vested portion to the beneficiary over time. Vesting progresses linearly between a start and an end timestamp, and a cliff blocks any release before a chosen point. This is the standard model for employee equity, investor grants, and team token allocations. When to use Use this pattern when you want a one-time, fund-it-now / release-later schedule: full amount locked immediately, then unlocked proportionally over time. If you instead need continuous accrual with arbitrary withdrawals, see Streaming Payments. Prerequisites Rust stable and cargo Soroban CLI installed (setup guide) Basic familiarity with Soroban contracts and the soroban_sdk Understanding of Address authentication (require_auth) and the SAC token interface Architecture The contract stores a single VestingSchedule and exposes four public functions: TokenVesting Contract ├── initialize(funder, beneficiary, token, total_amount, cliff_time, end_time) ├── release() -> released_amount ├── schedule() -> VestingSchedule ├── vested_amount() -> amount └── releasable_amount() -> amount Vesting Schedule Record​ pub struct VestingSchedule { pub funder: Address, // Address that funded the schedule pub beneficiary: Address, // Address entitled to release vested tokens pub token: Address, // Stellar asset contract held by this contract pub start_time: u64, // Ledger timestamp at which vesting began pub cliff_time: u64, // Earliest ledger timestamp a release is allowed pub end_time: u64, // Ledger timestamp at which the allocation is fully vested pub total_amount: i128, // Total tokens deposited for this schedule pub released_amount: i128, // Tokens already released to the beneficiary } Implementation ⚠️ Unaudited Example — Not for Production Use The contract code on this page is a teaching example and has not been audited. Do not deploy it as-is with real funds or in a production environment. Before using any vesting logic live, obtain a professional security audit, add support for schedule revocation / clawback if required, validate that the token contract is a trusted SAC-compliant implementation, and verify all edge cases (multiple schedules, very large total amounts, and timestamps far into the future). Reentrancy Soroban does not allow recursive or reentrant cross-contract calls within a single transaction, so the classic reentrancy pattern (where an external callback drains state before the original call finishes) is not possible on this platform. This vesting contract does invoke an external token contract during initialize (to pull funds from the funder) and during release (to pay the beneficiary), but because the state mutation (storing the schedule or updating released_amount) is applied before the token transfer, the Checks-Effects-Interactions ordering is preserved. If you extend this contract (e.g., add reward hooks, referral logic, or extra cross-contract calls), keep the authorization checks, state updates, and external call ordering under review. Storage TTL / Data Expiry This example stores the VestingSchedule in instance storage (env.storage().instance()). Instance entries live for the lifetime of the contract instance and do not need manual TTL bumps. There are no per-user persistent entries in the base pattern. If you extend the contract to use persistent storage (env.storage().persistent()) for additional records (e.g., per-beneficiary ledgers, audit trails, or multi-schedule maps), remember that persistent entries have a time-to-live (TTL) measured in ledgers and will expire if not read or written within ~120,000 ledgers (roughly 17 days on the public Stellar network). In that case call env.storage().persistent().bump(...) or extend_ttl after each read and write so records persist beyond the vesting horizon. The Vesting Math​ The core is a single pure function, vested_at, which returns how many tokens are vested at a given ledger timestamp: fn vested_at(schedule: &VestingSchedule, timestamp: u64) -> Result<i128, Error> { // Before the cliff nothing has vested. if timestamp < schedule.cliff_time { return Ok(0); } // At/after the end, the whole allocation is vested. if timestamp >= schedule.end_time { return Ok(schedule.total_amount); } let elapsed = i128::from(timestamp - schedule.start_time); let duration = i128::from(schedule.end_time - schedule.start_time); // total_amount * elapsed can overflow when total_amount is near i128::MAX. schedule .total_amount .checked_mul(elapsed) .map(|product| product / duration) .ok_or(Error::ArithmeticOverflow) } In the linear phase the vested amount is: vested(t) = floor( total_amount * (t - start_time) / (end_time - start_time) ) Integer division and the end-time fast path The contract computes total * elapsed / duration with integer arithmetic, so the final division is rounded down. That is why releasable_amount() can be non-zero right up to end_time, and why end_time uses a fast path that returns total_amount directly — guaranteeing the entire allocation (including any remainder from integer division) is released exactly at end_time. The multiplication uses checked_mul and returns Error::ArithmeticOverflow when total_amount × elapsed would exceed i128::MAX. Initialize​ The funder creates and funds the schedule in one call. The vesting start is the current ledger timestamp, so the funder controls when the clock starts by when they call initialize: pub fn initialize( env: Env, funder: Address, beneficiary: Address, token: Address, total_amount: i128, cliff_time: u64, end_time: u64, ) -> Result<(), Error> { if env.storage().instance().has(&DataKey::Schedule) { return Err(Error::AlreadyInitialized); } if total_amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } let start_time = env.ledger().timestamp(); if cliff_time < start_time || end_time <= cliff_time { return Err(Error::InvalidSchedule); } funder.require_auth(); // only the funder may create the schedule // ... persist the schedule ... token::Client::new(&env, &token).transfer( &funder, &env.current_contract_address(), &total_amount, ); Ok(()) } Release​ Only the beneficiary may release, and only the newly vested portion is paid each time: pub fn release(env: Env) -> Result<i128, Error> { let mut schedule = Self::load_schedule(&env)?; schedule.beneficiary.require_auth(); // only the beneficiary may release let now = env.ledger().timestamp(); if now < schedule.cliff_time { return Err(Error::CliffNotReached); } let vested = Self::vested_at(&schedule, now)?; let releasable = vested .checked_sub(schedule.released_amount) .ok_or(Error::ArithmeticOverflow)?; if releasable <= 0 { return Err(Error::NothingToRelease); } schedule.released_amount = vested; // track total vested so far // ... persist the schedule, then transfer `releasable` to the beneficiary ... Ok(releasable) } View Functions​ schedule() returns the full schedule, vested_amount() returns vested_at(now), and releasable_amount() returns vested - released (or 0 before the cliff). All three return Error::NotInitialized if no schedule exists yet. Key Properties​ Before the cliff: vested = 0, release returns Error::CliffNotReached. In the linear phase: vested = total * (t - start) / (end - start), rounded down. At/after end_time: vested = total — the full allocation, including any integer-division remainder. Each release pays only the delta: releasable = vested - released, so no token is ever released twice. One schedule, one fund: re-initialize returns Error::AlreadyInitialized. Authorization Action Authorized actor Check initialize Funder (the account funding the schedule) funder.require_auth() release Beneficiary (the account receiving tokens) beneficiary.require_auth() There is no separate admin role: the funder acts as the "admin" by being the only actor who can create and fund the schedule, and only the beneficiary can ever move tokens out of it. Time checks use the current ledger timestamp (env.ledger().timestamp()), so nobody can release early by supplying their own clock. Testing Run the example tests from the repository root (the same command CI runs): ./scripts/test-examples.sh token-vesting # or directly: cargo test --manifest-path examples/token-vesting/Cargo.toml The contract ships with tests covering the full schedule lifecycle and the overflow boundary: initialize funds the contract and records the schedule initialize rejects invalid amounts, invalid schedules, and re-initialization release is blocked before the cliff release at the cliff pays exactly the linearly vested portion Repeated releases transfer only newly vested tokens At end_time the full allocation is released exactly once vested_at returns ArithmeticOverflow for i128::MAX amounts mid-schedule vested_at at end_time returns i128::MAX without overflowing releasable_amount propagates overflow Boundary: a total amount just below the overflow threshold computes correctly View functions (schedule/vested_amount/releasable_amount) require initialization Security Considerations Overflow handling: total_amount × elapsed can overflow when the amount is near i128::MAX. The contract uses checked_mul and surfaces ArithmeticOverflow rather than silently wrapping. Cliff validation: cliff_time must be at or after the actual start (cliff_time < start_time is rejected) and end_time must be strictly after the cliff. Combined with start_time being the ledger timestamp, this prevents back-dated schedules. Single funding: the schedule is stored once; a second initialize is rejected, so the funder cannot "top up" or accidentally overwrite a schedule. Trust model: the funder must be trusted to fund the full amount up front (the transfer is part of initialize). The beneficiary is fully trusted to release at their convenience — there is no withdrawal cap beyond the schedule itself. No cancellation: this contract has no cancel/revoke path. If you need clawback, look at the SAC admin clawback or a timelock variant. Vesting vs Streaming Aspect Token Vesting Streaming Payments Cliff Yes — nothing releases before the cliff No — accrual starts immediately Funds Full allocation funded up front Full allocation funded up front Withdrawals Discrete releases (release()) Continuous (withdraw() anytime) Use case Employee equity, investor grants Payroll, subscriptions Related Patterns Streaming Payments — linear accrual without a cliff Basic Token — the token interface this contract uses Timelock Vault — lock-and-release with absolute timestamps Authorization — require_auth access control Deployment Guide Build the Contract​ stellar contract build --manifest-path examples/token-vesting/Cargo.toml The optimised Wasm is written to examples/target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/token_vesting.wasm. Deploy to Testnet​ stellar contract deploy \ --wasm examples/target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/token_vesting.wasm \ --source my-testnet-account \ --network testnet Initialize​ stellar contract invoke \ --id CABC... \ --source funder-account \ --network testnet \ -- initialize \ --funder "$(stellar keys address funder-account)" \ --beneficiary GBBD...your-beneficiary \ --token CTOKEN... \ --total_amount 1000000000 \ --cliff_time $(...unix-seconds...) \ --end_time $(...unix-seconds...) Release​ The beneficiary invokes release with their own key: stellar contract invoke \ --id CABC... \ --source beneficiary-account \ --network testnet \ -- release See Deploy to Testnet for account setup and funding.

The vesting start is the current ledger timestamp, so the funder controls when the clock starts by when they call initialize: pub fn initialize( env: Env, funder: Address, beneficiary: Address, token: Address, total_amount: i128, cliff_time: u64, end_time: u64, ) -> Result<(), Error> { if env.storage().instance().has(&DataKey::Schedule) { return Err(Error::AlreadyInitialized); } if total_amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } let start_time = env.ledger().timestamp(); if cliff_time < start_time || end_time <= cliff_time { return Err(Error::InvalidSchedule); } funder.require_auth(); // only the funder may create the schedule // ... persist the schedule ... token::Client::new(&env, &token).transfer( &funder, &env.current_contract_address(), &total_amount, ); Ok(()) }

Only the beneficiary may release, and only the newly vested portion is paid each time: pub fn release(env: Env) -> Result<i128, Error> { let mut schedule = Self::load_schedule(&env)?; schedule.beneficiary.require_auth(); // only the beneficiary may release let now = env.ledger().timestamp(); if now < schedule.cliff_time { return Err(Error::CliffNotReached); } let vested = Self::vested_at(&schedule, now)?; let releasable = vested .checked_sub(schedule.released_amount) .ok_or(Error::ArithmeticOverflow)?; if releasable <= 0 { return Err(Error::NothingToRelease); } schedule.released_amount = vested; // track total vested so far // ... persist the schedule, then transfer `releasable` to the beneficiary ... Ok(releasable) }

schedule() returns the full schedule, vested_amount() returns vested_at(now), and releasable_amount() returns vested - released (or 0 before the cliff). All three return Error::NotInitialized if no schedule exists yet.

Before the cliff: vested = 0, release returns Error::CliffNotReached. In the linear phase: vested = total * (t - start) / (end - start), rounded down. At/after end_time: vested = total — the full allocation, including any integer-division remainder. Each release pays only the delta: releasable = vested - released, so no token is ever released twice. One schedule, one fund: re-initialize returns Error::AlreadyInitialized.

Action Authorized actor Check initialize Funder (the account funding the schedule) funder.require_auth() release Beneficiary (the account receiving tokens) beneficiary.require_auth() There is no separate admin role: the funder acts as the "admin" by being the only actor who can create and fund the schedule, and only the beneficiary can ever move tokens out of it. Time checks use the current ledger timestamp (env.ledger().timestamp()), so nobody can release early by supplying their own clock.

Run the example tests from the repository root (the same command CI runs): ./scripts/test-examples.sh token-vesting # or directly: cargo test --manifest-path examples/token-vesting/Cargo.toml The contract ships with tests covering the full schedule lifecycle and the overflow boundary: initialize funds the contract and records the schedule initialize rejects invalid amounts, invalid schedules, and re-initialization release is blocked before the cliff release at the cliff pays exactly the linearly vested portion Repeated releases transfer only newly vested tokens At end_time the full allocation is released exactly once vested_at returns ArithmeticOverflow for i128::MAX amounts mid-schedule vested_at at end_time returns i128::MAX without overflowing releasable_amount propagates overflow Boundary: a total amount just below the overflow threshold computes correctly View functions (schedule/vested_amount/releasable_amount) require initialization

Overflow handling: total_amount × elapsed can overflow when the amount is near i128::MAX. The contract uses checked_mul and surfaces ArithmeticOverflow rather than silently wrapping. Cliff validation: cliff_time must be at or after the actual start (cliff_time < start_time is rejected) and end_time must be strictly after the cliff. Combined with start_time being the ledger timestamp, this prevents back-dated schedules. Single funding: the schedule is stored once; a second initialize is rejected, so the funder cannot "top up" or accidentally overwrite a schedule. Trust model: the funder must be trusted to fund the full amount up front (the transfer is part of initialize). The beneficiary is fully trusted to release at their convenience — there is no withdrawal cap beyond the schedule itself. No cancellation: this contract has no cancel/revoke path. If you need clawback, look at the SAC admin clawback or a timelock variant.

Aspect Token Vesting Streaming Payments Cliff Yes — nothing releases before the cliff No — accrual starts immediately Funds Full allocation funded up front Full allocation funded up front Withdrawals Discrete releases (release()) Continuous (withdraw() anytime) Use case Employee equity, investor grants Payroll, subscriptions

Streaming Payments — linear accrual without a cliff Basic Token — the token interface this contract uses Timelock Vault — lock-and-release with absolute timestamps Authorization — require_auth access control

intermediate☆ Category token Pattern ID token-wrapper Status stable Last reviewed August 2026

Token wrappers let an application hold an underlying asset and represent it as a custom Soroban token with additional policy logic. This pattern is a compact example of a wrapper that charges a fee on every transfer and routes the collected amount to a treasury address. The pattern is intentionally small: it focuses on three decisions that matter in production token contracts: validating fee configuration during initialization calculating a transfer fee before forwarding net value preserving a clear ledger of balances for both users and treasury

The wrapper stores: Balance(Address) entries for each address a configured Treasury address a FeeBps value expressed in basis points When a transfer is executed, the contract calculates: let fee = amount * fee_bps as i128 / 10_000; let net = amount - fee; It then debits the sender for the full amount, credits the recipient for the net amount, and credits the treasury for the fee portion. ⚠️ Unaudited Example — Not for Production Use The contract code on this page is a teaching example and has not been audited. Do not deploy it as-is with real funds or in a production environment. Before using any wrapper or fee-on-transfer logic live, obtain a professional security audit, add comprehensive error handling, apply access controls for minting, and verify all edge cases (including rounding, zero-fee transfers, and large-value arithmetic). Reentrancy Soroban does not allow recursive or reentrant cross-contract calls within a single transaction, so the classic reentrancy pattern (where an external callback drains state before the original call finishes) is not possible on this platform. Additionally, this wrapper example does not invoke any external contracts during transfer or mint, so there is no call-out surface where a callback could occur. If you extend this wrapper to interact with external contracts (e.g., hooking into a staking or rewards module), carefully review the authorization and balance-update ordering for every new call path. Storage TTL / Data Expiry This example uses two storage kinds: Instance storage (env.storage().instance()) for Treasury and FeeBps. Instance entries live for the lifetime of the contract instance and do not need manual TTL bumps. Persistent storage (env.storage().persistent()) for each user's Balance(Address). Persistent entries have a time-to-live (TTL) measured in ledgers and will expire if not read or written within ~120,000 ledgers (roughly 17 days on the public Stellar network). The example code never explicitly extends TTL, so a balance entry for a dormant user can be garbage-collected. For production use, call env.storage().persistent().bump(&key, &threshold, &extend_to) (or extend_ttl on the storage) after each read and write to ensure balances and accounting records persist for the required horizon.

init validates the treasury address and fee configuration before writing state. pub fn init(env: Env, treasury: Address, fee_bps: u32) -> Result<(), Error> { if env.storage().instance().has(&DataKey::Treasury) { return Err(Error::AlreadyInitialized); } if fee_bps > 10_000 { return Err(Error::InvalidFeeBps); } env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::Treasury, &treasury); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::FeeBps, &fee_bps); Ok(()) } This protects against invalid fee configuration and duplicate initialization.

The pattern rejects values above 10_000 because a basis-point fee greater than 100% is nonsensical for a token wrapper. The example also verifies that the amount itself is positive before transferring. if fee_bps > 10_000 { return Err(Error::InvalidFeeBps); } if amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); }

The wrapper enforces authorization from the sender and checks that the sender has enough balance to cover the full transfer amount. from.require_auth(); let from_balance = Self::get_balance(&env, &from_key); if from_balance < amount { return Err(Error::InsufficientBalance); } Then it computes fees and updates the balances in a single transfer flow.

Contract Tests #![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contracterror, contractimpl, contracttype, Address, Env}; #[contracttype] #[derive(Clone)] pub enum DataKey { Balance(Address), Treasury, FeeBps, } #[contracterror] #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq, PartialOrd, Ord)] #[repr(u32)] pub enum Error { AlreadyInitialized = 1, InvalidFeeBps = 2, InvalidAmount = 3, InsufficientBalance = 4, } #[contract] pub struct TokenWrapper; #[contractimpl] impl TokenWrapper { pub fn init(env: Env, treasury: Address, fee_bps: u32) -> Result<(), Error> { if env.storage().instance().has(&DataKey::Treasury) { return Err(Error::AlreadyInitialized); } if fee_bps > 10_000 { return Err(Error::InvalidFeeBps); } env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::Treasury, &treasury); env.storage().instance().set(&DataKey::FeeBps, &fee_bps); Ok(()) } pub fn mint(env: Env, to: Address, amount: i128) -> Result<(), Error> { if amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } let key = DataKey::Balance(to); let current = Self::get_balance(&env, &key); env.storage().persistent().set(&key, &(current + amount)); Ok(()) } pub fn balance(env: Env, of: Address) -> i128 { Self::get_balance(&env, &DataKey::Balance(of)) } pub fn transfer(env: Env, from: Address, to: Address, amount: i128) -> Result<(), Error> { from.require_auth(); if amount <= 0 { return Err(Error::InvalidAmount); } let from_key = DataKey::Balance(from.clone()); let from_balance = Self::get_balance(&env, &from_key); if from_balance < amount { return Err(Error::InsufficientBalance); } let treasury: Address = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::Treasury).unwrap(); let fee_bps: u32 = env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::FeeBps).unwrap_or(0); let fee = amount * fee_bps as i128 / 10_000; let net = amount - fee; let to_key = DataKey::Balance(to); let treasury_key = DataKey::Balance(treasury); let to_balance = Self::get_balance(&env, &to_key); let treasury_balance = Self::get_balance(&env, &treasury_key); env.storage().persistent().set(&from_key, &(from_balance - amount)); env.storage().persistent().set(&to_key, &(to_balance + net)); env.storage().persistent().set(&treasury_key, &(treasury_balance + fee)); Ok(()) } pub fn fee_bps(env: Env) -> u32 { env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::FeeBps).unwrap_or(0) } pub fn treasury(env: Env) -> Address { env.storage().instance().get(&DataKey::Treasury).unwrap() } fn get_balance(env: &Env, key: &DataKey) -> i128 { env.storage().persistent().get(key).unwrap_or(0) } } #[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; use soroban_sdk::{testutils::Address as _, Address, Env}; fn setup() -> (Env, TokenWrapperClient<'static>, Address, Address, Address) { let env = Env::default(); env.mock_all_auths(); let contract_id = env.register(TokenWrapper, ()); let client = TokenWrapperClient::new(&env, &contract_id); let alice = Address::generate(&env); let bob = Address::generate(&env); let treasury = Address::generate(&env); (env, client, alice, bob, treasury) } #[test] fn transfer_applies_fee_to_treasury() { let (_env, client, alice, bob, treasury) = setup(); client.init(&treasury, &100); client.mint(&alice, &1_000); client.transfer(&alice, &bob, &500); assert_eq!(client.balance(&alice), 500); assert_eq!(client.balance(&bob), 495); assert_eq!(client.balance(&treasury), 5); } #[test] fn init_rejects_invalid_fee() { let (_env, client, _alice, _bob, treasury) = setup(); let result = client.try_init(&treasury, &20_000); assert_eq!(result, Err(Ok(Error::InvalidFeeBps))); } }

Wrapper contracts are often used when a protocol needs to represent an external asset or enforce a specific policy on transfer flows without re-implementing the entire token standard from scratch. This example is a helpful stepping stone for: fee-on-transfer token mechanics treasury accounting and revenue sharing storing metadata and policy configuration in instance storage

The Soroban Cookbook ships a small, dependency-free experiment framework. This page is the process half of it: no experiment may be enabled until a plan following this template has been approved in a GitHub issue. The code half lives in src/utils/experiments.ts and src/hooks/useExperiment.ts.

We evaluated hosted experimentation platforms and chose not to adopt one yet: Consideration Hosted platform This framework Extra JS on every page 30–60 KB 0 KB Third-party origin in CSP Required None Cost at our traffic Free tier, then paid Free Statistical analysis Built in Manual, in GA4 Setup for one experiment Account, project, SDK Add a registry entry For a docs site running at most one or two experiments at a time, the hosted tooling costs more (in page weight and privacy surface) than the analysis convenience is worth. If we ever need sequential testing or automated significance calls, revisit this — PostHog is the likely choice because it can be self-hosted and its feature-flag API maps cleanly onto getVariant().

A random visitor ID is stored in localStorage under sc-visitor-id. It is not derived from any personal data and is never sent anywhere. The variant is FNV1a(experimentId + ":" + visitorId) % variants.length, so assignment is deterministic — a visitor sees the same variant on every page and on repeat visits — and independent across experiments. trafficAllocation gates what share of visitors enter at all. Visitors who decline analytics consent still get a stable variant (so the page does not flicker between visits) but generate no exposure events. Their behavior is therefore not measured, which is the intended trade-off. If localStorage is unavailable, the visitor always gets the control.

Append ?exp_<experiment_id>=<variant> to any URL — for example /?exp_hero_cta_copy=start_building. This works regardless of whether the experiment is enabled, which makes it the way to review a variant in a PR.

Copy this into the experiment's tracking issue. An experiment is not approved until a maintainer has signed off on a completed version of this. ### Experiment: <name> **Hypothesis** Changing <X> will improve <metric> because <reasoning>. **Variants** - `control`: <current behavior> - `<variant>`: <proposed behavior> **Primary metric** <single GA4 event or funnel step this is judged on> **Guardrail metrics** <what must not get worse — e.g. bounce rate, search usage> **Traffic allocation** <percentage, and why> **Minimum sample size** <visitors per variant, from a power calculation> **Planned duration** <at least one full week, to cover weekday/weekend cycles> **Decision rule** Ship <variant> if <metric> improves by ≥<threshold> with no guardrail regression. Otherwise keep control and record the finding. **Approved by** <maintainer> on <date>

This site's traffic is modest. Most plausible CTA changes produce effects small enough that a week of data cannot distinguish them from noise. Calculating the required sample before running tells you whether the experiment is worth running at all — and stops the far more common failure mode of watching a dashboard until the numbers happen to look good, which reliably manufactures false positives.
documents.s: Why a minimum sample size is mandatory

documents.t: Write the plan in a GitHub issue using the template above. Get sign-off. Add the registry entry in src/utils/experiments.ts with enabled: false: myExperiment: { id: 'my_experiment', variants: ['control', 'treatment'], enabled: false, trafficAllocation: 100, hypothesis: '…', }, Implement both variants behind the hook: const variant = useExperiment('myExperiment'); return variant === 'treatment' ? <Treatment /> : <Control />; Review both using the ?exp_my_experiment=treatment override. Enable in a separate, easily reverted PR flipping enabled: true. Wait for the planned duration. Do not peek-and-stop early. Analyze in GA4 (see below), then conclude: ship the winner by making it the only code path, and delete the experiment entry. Leaving concluded experiments in the registry is how a codebase accumulates permanent dead branches — removal is part of finishing.

Each assignment emits experiment_exposure with experiment_id and variant. Register both as custom dimensions (Admin → Custom definitions), then: Explore → Free form. Breakdown dimension: variant. Metric: the primary metric from the plan (e.g. funnel_cta_click count). Filter: experiment_id equals your experiment. Compare the conversion rate per variant — exposures are the denominator, not sessions. GA4 will not test significance for you; use an external two-proportion z-test calculator with the exposure and conversion counts. See DEPLOYMENT.md → Analytics for the underlying event catalog.

Never experiment on documentation correctness. Layout, copy, and navigation are fair game; the accuracy of a contract example is not. Never run two experiments that touch the same element. Assignment is independent, so overlapping experiments make effects uninterpretable. Accessibility is not a variant. Every variant must meet the same a11y bar. No experiment may block first paint. Variants resolve after mount, so design them to swap in without layout shift.

documents.t: Plan the interactive code playground feature for the Soroban Cookbook. This document defines requirements, evaluates technical architectures, proposes UI/UX mockups, identifies integration points, and establishes a timeline and milestones.

In-browser code editing: Allow users to edit Rust/Soroban code snippets directly in the browser. Compilation: Compile Rust code to WASM either in-browser or via a remote API. Execution: Execute the compiled WASM in a sandboxed environment and display the result. Integration: Embed playground components into MDX documentation pages. MVP scope: Support the hello-world example end-to-end (edit, compile, run, output).

Use crate soroban-sdk with wasm-bindgen and a Rust-to-WASM compiler (e.g. wasm-unknown-unknown target). Pros: No server cost, offline support, low latency. Cons: Large WASM bundle, browser compatibility issues, complex toolchain.

Build a backend service that receives Rust source and returns compiled WASM. Pros: Simpler frontend, full toolchain control, easier to update. Cons: Requires server infrastructure, network latency, potential scalability challenges. Decision: For the MVP, use a remote API (Option B) to avoid browser compilation complexity. Later, if needed, evaluate in-browser compilation as an enhancement.

A playground panel embedded below code snippets. Layout: Code editor on the left, output console on the right. Buttons: "Run", "Reset", "Copy". Editor: Monaco editor for Rust syntax highlighting. Output: Scrollable console showing stdout/stderr or compilation errors.

Docusaurus MDX: Create a <Playground> component to wrap code snippets. Reuse existing CodePreview component for read-only display. Add a "Run in Playground" button to code blocks via Docusaurus theme extension or custom MDX components. Build a small HTTP API endpoint for compilation/execution.

Milestone Description Estimated Time M1 Requirements and architecture finalized Week 1 M2 Backend compilation service prototype Week 2 M3 Frontend playground component integration Week 3 M4 MVP complete: hello-world compiles and runs Week 4
The Phase 4 MVP delivers read-only code preview with syntax highlighting for Rust/Soroban code snippets embedded in documentation pages.

Feature Details CodePreview component Reusable React component at src/components/CodePreview/index.tsx Syntax highlighting Prism-based via prism-react-renderer (already a project dependency) Copy-to-clipboard One-click copy with visual feedback (Copied! confirmation) Line numbers Shown by default, toggleable via showLineNumbers prop Collapsible long blocks Optional collapseAt prop to collapse code exceeding N lines MDX usage <CodePreview language="rust" code={...} title="lib.rs" />

interface CodePreviewProps { code: string; // Required — the code to render language?: string; // Default: 'rust' fileName?: string; // Displayed in the header bar title?: string; // Alternative header label (takes precedence over fileName) className?: string; // Custom CSS class showLineNumbers?: boolean; // Default: true collapseAt?: number; // 0 = no collapse; N = collapse after N lines }

import { CodePreview } from '@site/src/components/CodePreview'; <CodePreview language="rust" title="hello-world/src/lib.rs" code={`#![no_std] use soroban_sdk::{contract, contractimpl, Env, String}; #[contract] pub struct HelloWorld; #[contractimpl] impl HelloWorld { pub fn hello(env: Env) -> String { env.storage().instance().get(&String::from_str(&env, "msg")).unwrap_or( String::from_str(&env, "Hello, Soroban!"), ) } }`} />

Docusaurus already ships with Prism support and prism-react-renderer as a dependency. Prism has a comprehensive Rust grammar (additionalLanguages: ['rust'] is already configured in docusaurus.config.ts). No new dependencies were added — the component uses only what the project already includes.

The existing CodeSnippet component focuses on interactive code features (comment toggling, file download, tabbed multi-snippet views). CodePreview is a lighter-weight component purpose-built for the Phase 4 MVP: read-only syntax highlighting with copy-to-clipboard. Keeping them separate avoids bloating CodePreview with features it doesn't need, and avoids breaking changes to CodeSnippet's existing API.
documents.s: Why a new component instead of extending CodeSnippet?

documents.t: react-syntax-highlighter is a heavier dependency that bundles multiple highlighter engines. Since prism-react-renderer is already installed and provides the same Prism-based highlighting Docusaurus uses internally, adding another library would be redundant.

The following features are not part of this MVP and are tracked separately: WASM compile pipeline — Server-side compilation of Rust code to WASM. This requires a backend compilation API and is tracked as a separate Phase 4 item in the roadmap (#136). Live execution sandbox — Running compiled WASM in-browser (e.g. via wasmi or wasm-bindgen). Requires the compilation pipeline first. Interactive editing — Monaco editor integration, real-time compilation feedback. This is Phase 3 territory. Server-side execution API — A backend service that compiles and executes Soroban contracts. Separate roadmap item. Testnet deployment from browser — Deploying compiled contracts to Stellar testnet. Requires wallet integration and backend services.
